title: Edge
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree The fleet layer for a Multisite: several servers (edges) share one set of instances, any edge accepts any request, and a request for an instance another edge runs is forwarded there over the private network. Works with either runtime provider, pocker or docker. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Edge
heading: Install
text: Edge is built into pocketone . It turns on in host mode (a multisite section in pocketone.yaml ) when the file has an edges section, or a mothership section (Mothership), which lists the edges too. In your own Go build, give the host a router as its forward hook: edges, err := edge.FromSection(log) // the edges section; nil when there is none if edges != nil { opts.Forward = edge.NewRouter(edge.RouterConfig{Edges: edges, Logger: log}).Forward } h, err := multisite.FromConfig(opts) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/edge .

title: Edge
heading: Configure
text: The edges section names this edge and lists the others (keys below): edges: self: lax-1 list: { id: sgp-1, internal_url: "http://10.88.0.4:8080", region: sgp } server: plain: [":8080"] # where the other edges reach this one (their internal_url for it) Each entry needs id and internal_url . An instance another edge runs names its owner in remote : instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] remote: edge:@sgp-1 # also accepted: edge:sgp-1, or sgp-1 Without a mothership, instances come from the instances file. With one, instances and edges both come from it; a fixed edges.list entry wins over the mothership's for the same edge.

title: Edge
heading: edges:
text: The fleet: this edge's id and a fixed list of the other edges (id, internal_url, region). self string This edge's id, such as lax-1. list list of object The other edges: id, internal_url (where this edge reaches it) and optional region.

title: Edge
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to run by hand. A load balancer sends visitors to any edge, and each request ends up on the edge that runs its instance: Owner healthy: the request is forwarded to its internal_url , with the original hostname. An edge is healthy when its source heard from it in the last 30 seconds, or else when it answers /.well-known/health (an edge the source marks offline never is). Owner briefly unreachable but healthy: requests are held and retried every 250 ms until it answers. Only requests without a body (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) are replayed after a failed connection. Owner down or unknown: a 503 with Retry-After: 10 , at once. Never bounced: a request another edge already forwarded is never forwarded again; it gets a 421. CORS: for an instance with access.cors_origins , the entry edge answers preflights and sets the only Access-Control-Allow-Origin the browser sees. Headers: where both edges set the same header (such as the firewall's rate-limit headers), the owner's wins.

title: Edge
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Edge fills the host's forward hook for instances with remote set. Pocker, Docker Either runs the instances this edge owns; an app already running here stops when its instance moves to another edge. Firewall The entry edge checks the peer and the instance's rate limits before forwarding. Mothership Its mirror is an edge source: it follows the mothership's list of edges and their heartbeats.

title: Edge
heading: Building on Edge
text: Edge sources. Implement edge.EdgeSource ( Self , Resolve , Edges ) to say where the other edges are; add Run ( edge.Runner ) for background work. YAMLProvider is the edges.list one; MultiProvider combines several, the first to resolve an instance's remote winning. Router. edge.NewRouter(edge.RouterConfig{...}) takes the health path, healthy window, retry interval and the 503 and 421 messages. Plug Router.Forward into multisite.Host.Forward . Timing. edge.WithMark(ctx) records which edge a request was forwarded to and when, e.g. for Server-Timing.

title: Edge
heading: Example
text: Edge has no example program of its own. The stock binary wires it up in examples/pocketone/multi.go , together with the mothership's edge list.

title: Edge
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Firewall
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Peer allow-lists, trusted proxies and client IPs, and per-IP and per-instance rate limits for a Multisite, with or without Edge. Every request is checked before an instance serves it or it's forwarded to another edge. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Firewall
heading: Install
text: The firewall is built into pocketone . It turns on in host mode (a multisite section in pocketone.yaml ), as the host's gate/v1, when the file has a firewall or rate_limits section; there's nothing else to install. In your own Go build, importing the package registers it with the host, with the same rule: import _ "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/firewall" Or build one in Go and add it to the host's gates, as the example does. A single app doesn't need it: stock PocketBase has its own per-IP rate limits and trusted proxies.

title: Firewall
heading: Configure
text: Two sections, both optional; either one turns the firewall on (keys below). firewall: allow_cidrs: [] # peers allowed to connect (empty = everyone) trusted_proxies: [] # peers whose client-IP headers are believed client_ip_headers: [CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP] trusted_clients: [] # client IPs that get the trusted rate limits on every instance trusted_client_headers: [X-Client-IP] # a trusted client names its end user: each user gets their own limits rate_limit_header_prefix: X-RateLimit rate_limits: # defaults for every instance ip_hourly: 1000 instance_hourly: 10000 ip_concurrent: 15 instance_concurrent: 250 file_weight: 0.1 # a /api/files request costs a tenth trusted: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_hourly: 20000, ip_concurrent: 50, instance_concurrent: 250 } # off: true # no rate limiting The values shown are the defaults. In dev mode ( instances: { dev: true } ) rate limiting is off unless the file has a rate_limits section. A trusted limit is never lower than the normal one. Each instance can set its own limits and trusted IPs in its extensions.firewall settings; missing fields keep the defaults: instances: id: api hosts: [api.example.com] extensions: firewall: { rate_limits: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_concurrent: 500 }, trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] }

title: Firewall
heading: firewall:
text: Peers allowed to connect, trusted proxies and client-IP headers, trusted clients, the rate-limit header prefix. Turns the firewall on. allow_cidrs list of string Peers (IPs or CIDRs) allowed to connect; others get 403. Empty: everyone. trusted_proxies list of string Peers whose client-IP headers are believed. client_ip_headers list of string Headers read, in order, for the client IP from a trusted proxy. Default CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP. trusted_clients list of string Client IPs or CIDRs that get the trusted rate limits on every instance. trusted_client_headers list of string Headers a trusted client uses to name its end user's IP, so each user gets their own limits. Default X-Client-IP. rate_limit_header_prefix string Prefix of the rate-limit response headers. Default X-RateLimit.

title: Firewall
heading: rate_limits:
text: Default rate limits for every instance (per instance: extensions.firewall.rate_limits). Turns the firewall on. ip_hourly int Requests per hour from one client IP to one instance. Default 1000. instance_hourly int Requests per hour to one instance from everyone. Default 10000. ip_concurrent int Requests one client IP may have open on one instance at once. Default 15. instance_concurrent int Requests one instance may have open at once. Default 250. file_weight number What a /api/files request costs, as a share of a request. Default 0.1. trusted.ip_hourly int Requests per hour from one trusted client IP to one instance. trusted.instance_hourly int Requests per hour to one instance. trusted.ip_concurrent int Requests one trusted client IP may have open on one instance at once. trusted.instance_concurrent int Requests one instance may have open at once. off bool No rate limiting. The default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set.

title: Firewall
heading: Use
text: What callers see: Peers outside allow_cidrs get 403. Client IP: taken from client_ip_headers only when the peer is a trusted proxy; otherwise it's the peer. The app then sees that client as the request's IP, so PocketBase's logs and its own rate limits see the visitor. Over a limit: 429 with Retry-After and a message naming the limit and the IP. Every routed response carries X-RateLimit-{Ip,Instance}-{Hourly,Concurrent}-{Limit,Remaining} and X-RateLimit-{Ip,Instance}-Hourly-Reset (with your prefix), listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers so browser code can read them. Long-lived responses (realtime) count toward the concurrency limits until they end.

title: Firewall
heading: Trusted clients that serve many users
text: A trusted client (process-wide trusted_clients , or an instance's own trusted_ips ) that serves many users, such as a server-side proxy or SSR app, sends each request's end-user IP in a trusted_client_headers header. Per-IP limits then apply to that user, still with the trusted limits; without the header all its users share one bucket. The header is ignored from anyone else, so it can't be spoofed to escape a limit.

title: Firewall
heading: Works with
text: Multisite The firewall is a host gate: it checks the peer, then admits each request before the runtime or the forward hook. Pocker, Docker Either provider; the firewall runs in front of both. Edge The entry edge applies the limits before forwarding. The owner edge's rate-limit headers replace the entry edge's, since the owner counted every request for the instance. Multitenant (planned) Will write each instance's extensions.firewall settings, such as its owner's trusted IPs.

title: Firewall
heading: Building on the firewall
text: Per instance. Write extensions.firewall.rate_limits and extensions.firewall.trusted_ips into an instance's settings (from the instances file or your own instance source). Go API. firewall.Firewall{Config, RateLimits} is a multisite.Gate you can add to Host.Gates yourself; NewFirewall(cfg) builds one ready to use. ClientIP(r) gives a request's client. firewall.SectionAdjust changes the settings read from pocketone.yaml before the firewall is built.

title: Firewall
heading: Example
text: The firewall in front of a toy host: only 127.0.0.1 may connect, at 100 requests an hour per IP. Run it from this folder with go run ./example --instances instances.yaml . // The firewall in front of a host: every request is checked (allowed peers, rate limits) before a toy runtime // answers. In a PocketOne binary the firewall turns on from pocketone.yaml's firewall / rate_limits sections; here // it is built in Go. // // go run ./example --instances instances.yaml package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "net/http" "os" "os/signal" "syscall" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/multisite" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/firewall" ) type okRuntime struct{} func (okRuntime) Name() string { return "ok" } func (okRuntime) Serves(inst multisite.Instance) bool { return true } func (okRuntime) Ready() bool { return true } func (okRuntime) ServeInstance(w http.ResponseWriter, _ http.Request, inst multisite.Instance) { fmt.Fprintf(w, "hello from %s\n", inst.ID) } func main() { instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file") listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address") flag.Parse() fw := &firewall.Firewall{ Config: firewall.Config{AllowCIDRs: []string{"127.0.0.1"}}, RateLimits: &firewall.RateLimits{IPHourly: 100}, } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() h := &multisite.Host{Source: &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: instances}, Runtimes: []multisite.Runtime{okRuntime{}}, Gates: []multisite.Gate{fw}, Listeners: multisite.Listeners{Listen: listen}} if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit(1) } }

title: Firewall
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Extensions
text: Each extension is a Go module in ext/ with its own README; the pages here are those READMEs. Want to add one? Read Writing an extension.

title: Extensions
heading: Standard extensions
text: These ship with pocketone and add no work to an app that doesn't use them. Auto TLS Certificates on demand and wildcards through ACME. Backups Restore an app to a moment from its own backups: the latest one before it. On by default. Bulk Mail Campaigns to your app's own users, with audiences from a collection, a view or SQL. Cache Cache buckets for every app in the process from one shared store: identical values kept once, LRU/MRU/FIFO/LIFO eviction, TTLs, an optional disk tier. Config The pocketone.yaml config file, with secrets in a .env beside it. Deploy pocketone deploy, dev, pull and logs, and the deploy API. JSVM PocketOne's JS engine: one QuickJS VM per app, real globals, async handlers, hard limits. MCP An MCP endpoint at /mcp so agents can manage your app and call its tools. Pages Server-rendered pages from a pb_pages folder (formerly PocketPages). PITR Point-in-time restore of your database with Litestream. On by default. Remotes Named remotes and saved logins for the pocketone command. S3 Redirect File downloads as short-lived signed S3 redirects. Settings One API for the settings an app's admins change for its extensions. On by default. Templates Theme an extension's own pages (the OAuth sign-in screens): eject its templates to pb_templates and edit them. Tokens Long-lived API tokens with scopes. Upgrade pocketone upgrade to the latest release, keeping the old executable. Vacuum Compact your app's SQLite databases on a schedule, so space freed by deleted records goes back to the disk.

title: Extensions
heading: Run many instances
text: Host hundreds of PocketBase instances in one process, across regions. Docker A host provider that runs each instance in its own container. Edge Forwards each request to the edge that owns the instance. Firewall Peer allow-lists, trusted proxies and rate limits for a host. Mothership A control plane and its edges, across regions. Multisite Many instances behind one listener, routed by hostname, run by one provider. Pocker Hundreds of PocketBase instances in one Go process, routed by hostname. Sandbox Confines untrusted JS hooks, SQL and outbound network. Schedules Planned. Scheduled webhooks that wake sleeping instances. Stats Measures disk use and last request for each instance a host serves.

title: Extensions
heading: Services for your instances
text: Shared services a host gives every instance it runs. Mail Relay Outgoing mail for instances without SMTP, through your relay, with limits. S3 Fallback A default bucket for uploads and backups when an instance has no S3 of its own. Server Timing Server-Timing headers for each step of a request.

title: Extensions
heading: Sell it as a service
text: Accounts, quotas and billing, for running PocketBase as a service. Lemon Squeezy Adapter Planned. Lemon Squeezy as the billing provider. Multitenant Planned. Accounts that own instances: quotas, owner logins, tokens and an API. Multitenant Billing Planned. Plans, quotas and the billing provider hook for Multitenant.

title: Extensions
heading: For extension authors
text: The extension contract and tools for building and testing extensions. Bundle An app's hooks, migrations and public files embedded in the binary. Contracts The versioned interfaces extensions use to work together, and the generator that writes their plumbing. Dev Users Local testing only: a superuser and a user with password "password". Extension Kit The extension contract: one extension works on a single app and under pocker. Mail Trap Dev mode: mail from an app without SMTP lands in a built-in inbox. Standard Set The extensions every PocketOne app has, as one set a host configures.

title: JSVM
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree PocketOne's JS engine for pb_hooks and pb_migrations . It runs the same JS API as PocketBase ( $app , onX , routerAdd , cronAdd , $http , $security , ...) on QuickJS, with one VM per app: Real globals. Every hook file runs in the app's one global scope, so top-level helpers, constants and state are visible to every handler. No more require() inside each handler. ES modules. .pb.mjs (and TypeScript .pb.ts / .pb.mts ) hook files and modules use import / export , including top-level await ; .pb.js and .pb.cjs stay scripts with require() . Both share the same module instances. TypeScript. .ts , .mts and .cts hooks, migrations and modules run directly (types stripped by esbuild, linked into the binary), with error positions in your .ts source. Async. Handlers can be async . Every Go function has an .async(...) twin that runs off the VM and returns a promise, so one app serves other requests while it waits: await $app.findRecordById.async("posts", id) . Hard limits per app. A memory cap (JS heap plus Go objects JS holds), a CPU and a wall-clock budget per task, and caps on queued tasks and async calls. A runaway script stops with an error; other apps in the process keep running. Real error positions. Stack traces name pb_hooks/ : . The pocketone binary and every Pocker instance run on it. PocketBase's own plugins/jsvm (goja) is for pure PocketBase compatibility only: jsvm: goja under app: in pocketone.yaml (or --jsvm goja ) runs a single app on it, with pages, $mcp , $tokens , $bulkmail and JS contracts off. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: JSVM
heading: Install
text: The engine is pure Go (QuickJS translated to Go by modernc.org/libquickjs, the way PocketBase uses modernc.org/sqlite), so it needs no cgo: CGO_ENABLED=0 builds and cross-compiles work as with stock PocketBase. In your own Go build, register it where you'd register plugins/jsvm : jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"}) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm .

title: JSVM
heading: Configure
text: Config takes PocketBase's jsvm fields ( HooksDir , HooksWatch , HooksFilesPattern , MigrationsDir , MigrationsFilesPattern , TypesDir ; HooksPoolSize is accepted and ignored) plus: OnInit func(rt js.Runtime) : add globals after everything else is set up. VM : the limits. MemoryLimit (default 64 MiB), TaskBudget (JS time per task, default 5 s), TaskWall (wall time per task, Go calls included, default 30 s), QueueSize , MaxAsync , MaxPumpDepth . Array methods that walk every index ( join , indexOf , slice , forEach , concat , flat , ...) and arrays passed to Go throw a RangeError past MemoryLimit / 16 elements: QuickJS doesn't check TaskBudget inside those loops, and a sparse array ( new Array(1e9) ) or array-like costs no memory, so the cap is what stops them. No dense array that long fits in MemoryLimit . Extensions : values that extend it (below).

title: JSVM
heading: Use
text: Write hooks and migrations as in PocketBase's JS docs; they run unchanged. What's new: // pb_hooks/main.pb.js const cache = new Map() routerAdd("GET", "/post/{slug}", async (e) = { const slug = e.request.pathValue("slug") if (!cache.has(slug)) { cache.set(slug, await e.app.findFirstRecordByData.async("posts", "slug", slug)) } return e.json(200, cache.get(slug)) }) Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart, a hooks reload or running out of memory starts a fresh one, so keep durable data in the database. After an await , other requests may have run: use e.app , not the global $app , and keep transactions short across await s (they hold SQLite's write lock). Calls that wait on I/O ( $app methods, DB queries, $http.send , sleep ) let the app's other requests run even without .async . process.env and a small Buffer ( from , toString with utf8, base64, hex) are there.

title: JSVM
heading: Modules: import and require
text: Name a file for what it is: .mjs is an ES module, .cjs is CommonJS. A plain .js file is CommonJS, so existing PocketBase hooks run unchanged (inside node_modules , Node's rule applies: "type": "module" in the package's package.json makes its .js files ES modules). TypeScript is written as ES modules, so .ts and .mts are ES modules and .cts is the CommonJS exception. pb_hooks/ .pb.mjs , .pb.ts , .pb.mts ES module: import , export , top-level await , import.meta export / import ; its top-level names are private pb_hooks/ .pb.js , .pb.cjs , .pb.cts script in the app's one global scope, with require() globals pb_migrations/ .mjs , .ts , .mts ES module each migration has its own scope either way pb_migrations/ .js , .cjs , .cts script in its own function scope All of them run in the app's one VM: scripts and modules share the global object (a module can read a script's globals) and one instance of every module. // pb_hooks/lib/store.mjs export const state = { hits: 0 } export const bump = () = ++state.hits // pb_hooks/main.pb.mjs import { bump } from "./lib/store.mjs" import legacy from "./lib/legacy.cjs" // CommonJS: module.exports is the default export import { hello } from "some-package" // node_modules, CommonJS or ES const posts = await $app.findCollectionByNameOrId.async("posts") // top-level await: done before the app serves routerAdd("GET", "/hit", (e) = e.json(200, { hits: bump() })) import and require() resolve the same way: relative paths ( .js , .mjs , .cjs , .json and index. tried in turn), then node_modules packages by package.json exports (the import or require condition) or main . A module loads once per app, however many files import or require it, so its state is shared by every request. Importing a CommonJS module gives its module.exports as the default export, its keys as named exports, and the same instance require() returns. require() of an ES module returns its namespace (the same instance import gives), as in Node 22, as long as the module has no top-level await ; for one that does, use await import("./lib/x.mjs") .

title: JSVM
heading: TypeScript
text: .ts , .mts and .cts files run as they are: esbuild strips the types when the file loads, and each file's source map is kept, so an error names pb_hooks/main.pb.mts:12:5 in your source, not in the stripped code. There's no type checking at runtime. Check with tsc --noEmit or your editor; pb_data/types.d.ts types the whole JS API. Imports may name the compiled file, as TypeScript's NodeNext style does: import { add } from "./math.js" loads math.ts when there's no math.js . import type and other type-only imports disappear, so a .pb.cts script can use them and stay a script. A .cts module may still be written with import / export ; it's turned into CommonJS.

title: JSVM
heading: Types
text: When the app starts, pb_data/types.d.ts gets the declarations of the whole JS API, for your editor and tsc : PocketBase's API generated from PocketOne's core (its extra hooks included), by PocketBase's own generator. What this engine adds ( pocketone.d.ts ): .async on every Go function, fully typed ( await $app.findRecordById.async(...) is a Promise ), require , process , Buffer , console , import.meta . Each extension's own API, for the extensions on in that app ( $mcp , $tokens , $bulkmail , onContracts and the contracts' action hooks). To type-check, point a tsconfig.json at it: { "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2022", "module": "ESNext", "moduleResolution": "Bundler", "lib": ["ES2022"], "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "allowImportingTsExtensions": true, "skipLibCheck": true }, "include": ["pb_data/types.d.ts", "pb_hooks/ / ", "pb_migrations/ / "] } skipLibCheck skips two type errors inside PocketBase's own generated declarations. In a PocketOne checkout, go generate in ext/jsvm regenerates the declarations after a core change (the TestTypes tests fail until you do).

title: JSVM
heading: Integrations
text: Extensions plug in through Config.Extensions with the engine-neutral types in ext/extkit/js . A value implements any of: OnInit(rt) : set up the VM. BindJS(app, rt) : expose a Go API. TypeScript() : declare it for editors and tsc (appended to pb_data/types.d.ts ). OnCall(rt) : wrap every handler call; an error refuses it. HTTPClient(rt) : the client $http.send uses. HookFiles , MigrationFiles , Modules : hooks, migrations and require() modules from somewhere other than disk. OnLoad(rt, root, file, content) : wrap loading each hook file. js.Run(app, fn) runs Go code on the app's VM; a js.Func kept from JS can be called from any goroutine. Bundle uses these to serve hooks and migrations embedded in the binary.

title: JSVM
heading: Example
text: // Command example serves example/pb_hooks with the jsvm extension: one QuickJS VM for the app, so the hook file's // top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler. // // cd example && go run . serve // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello/world package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: JSVM
heading: How it works
text: Each app's VM is owned by one goroutine, its loop; everything that touches the VM runs there. Go code elsewhere posts tasks and waits. A Go call made from JS that fires a hook runs it inline, so Go → JS → Go → JS works. Go values cross live through two QuickJS classes: GoObject (property get/set/has/keys go to Go by reflection, with PocketBase's JS names) and GoFunc (calls go to Go). Each holds a handle into the VM's table; QuickJS's refcounting frees it as soon as JS drops it. Memory: QuickJS caps its own heap. Go objects JS holds are charged to the same budget: a per-type estimate, and a reachability walk for fresh results of Go calls. QuickJS is modernc.org/libquickjs, Bellard's QuickJS translated to Go, so there is no cgo. It runs about as fast as goja; deep recursion stops at VM.StackSize (QuickJS stack slots, about one per call; default 5000) with "InternalError: stack overflow". Benchmarks and the red team (27 attacks against 50 VMs in one process) are in the package's tests ( ASYNCVM_BENCH=1 , ASYNCVM_REDTEAM=1 ).

text: MIT

title: Mail Relay
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Outgoing mail for Pocker instances that haven't set up SMTP. Stock PocketBase falls back to the host's sendmail when SMTP is off. Under Pocker that would run sendmail on the shared host for every tenant. With this extension: SMTP on in an instance's Settings → Mail: the app sends the mail itself. Bring your own SMTP always wins. SMTP off: the mail goes through your relay as @ , within per-instance limits. sendmail never runs. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mail Relay
heading: Install
text: Mail Relay is not in the pocketone binary. Add it to the extensions of your own Pocker build, with your sending domain and relay: srv.Extensions = append(srv.Extensions, mailrelay.New(mailrelay.Config{ Domain: "mail.example.com", Upstream: mailrelay.SMTPUpstream{Addr: "smtp.provider.com:587", Username: "…", Password: "…"}, })) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailrelay . It works the same in pocker.Provider{Extensions: ...} . It also registers on a single app, but a single app can set up its own SMTP and doesn't need a relay.

title: Mail Relay
heading: The relay (Go)
text: Domain and Upstream are required; the host doesn't start without them. Domain : every relayed message is From @Domain . Upstream : what delivers the mail. SMTPUpstream ships here: Addr (host:port), optional Username and Password (PLAIN auth, only over TLS or to localhost), ImplicitTLS for port 465 (otherwise STARTTLS when the server offers it), and Timeout (default 30 s). It dials with its own dialer, so Pocker's egress rules for tenants (public addresses only) don't block a relay on a private address. Anything with Send(ctx, from, to, raw) works, for example an Amazon SES SendRawEmail sender. LocalPart : picks an instance's address from its id. The default is the first label of the id, lowercased: blog.localhost → blog . Limits: PerMinute (default 20) and Daily (default 200) per instance, MaxRecipients (To + Cc + Bcc, default 5) and MaxSize (encoded message, default 1 MiB) per message.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Defaults for every instance (pocketone.yaml)
text: mailrelay: { per_minute: 20, daily: 200 } Limits set in Go win over this section. Each instance can override it (see Per-instance settings).

title: Mail Relay
heading: Use
text: Once it's in, there's nothing to run. Each instance's mail is relayed whenever its SMTP is off. Settings → Mail in an instance's dashboard shows its superusers the relay: the address it sends as, its limits and how many messages it sent today. When sending is off for the instance, it says so and points to the SMTP settings. The app's log (Admin Logs, which Pocker copies to the instance's own log) gets one line per message, with masked addresses: mailrelay: sent from=blog@… to=a @x.org . Refusals and upstream failures are warnings. A refused message returns an error to whoever triggered the mail, such as a password-reset request: sending off, too many recipients, too large, or the limit reached.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Works with
text: Contracts Provides mail.fallback/v1 : with SMTP off, an app's mail goes to the contract's providers in order ( providers: { mail.fallback/v1: [mailtrap, mailrelay] } ); Mail Relay sends it within the instance's limits. Pocker The host it's built for. Every instance gets the relay, its own address and its own limits. Mail Trap In development, point SMTPUpstream at the trap's SMTP port and every relayed message lands in one inbox, tagged with the instance. The example below does this. Bulk Mail Campaigns go through PocketBase's mailer by default, so with SMTP off they are relayed and count against the instance's limits.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: Each instance can override the defaults in its extensions.mailrelay settings, from instances.yaml or your instance source (for example, per plan): instances: id: free-plan-app extensions: { mailrelay: { send: false } } # refuse its mail unless it uses its own SMTP id: big-app extensions: { mailrelay: { per_minute: 60, daily: 2000 } } A change to these settings restarts the instance's app on its next request. Use send: false , not enabled: false , to stop an instance sending. enabled: false turns the extension off for that instance, and with SMTP off PocketBase then falls back to the host's sendmail . Don't set it under Pocker.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Building on Mail Relay
text: Your own upstream. Implement mailrelay.Upstream ( Send(ctx, from, to, raw) ) to deliver through an API. Your own hooks first. The relay runs after the app's own onMailerSend hooks, so they can still change or drop a message. Go API. ( mailrelay.Extension).Address(id) returns the From address an instance sends as. settings/v1 (superusers): GET /api/_c/settings/v1/get?extension=mailrelay returns the instance's relay status, a read-only section: active , send , address , perMinute , daily , sentToday .

title: Mail Relay
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs a Pocker host whose relay sends to the dev mail trap, so every instance's mail lands in one inbox at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Run go run ./example --dev from this folder, then trigger a password reset on any instance: curl -X POST http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com Log in to an instance's dashboard as admin@example.com / password to see the relay on Settings → Mail. --listen changes the instances' port; P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP and P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP change the trap's. // Command example is a Pocker build with mailrelay, relaying into PocketOne's dev mail trap: every instance // without its own SMTP sends as @mail.localhost, and all of it lands in one inbox. // // go run ./example --dev // // Then trigger mail on any instance, for example a password reset (each instance has the test user below): // // curl -X POST http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com // curl -X POST http://beta.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com // // and read it in PocketOne's dev mail trap at http://127.0.0.1:8025 (filter by instance; P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP and // P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP change its ports). Settings → Mail in each dashboard shows the relay. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "context" "flag" "log" "os" "os/signal" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailrelay" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pocker" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/standard" ) func main() { dev := flag.Bool("dev", false, "serve any hostname (alpha.localhost, beta.localhost, ...); otherwise instances.yaml is required") listen := flag.String("listen", "", "HTTP address for the instances (default :8090)") flag.Parse() cfg := pocker.DefaultConfig() cfg.Dev = cfg.Dev dev if listen != "" { cfg.Listen = listen } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt) defer stop() // The dev mail trap (ext/mailtrap) stands in for the operator's real relay (SES, a provider's SMTP, ...) inbox, err := mailtrap.Default("mailrelay example: the relay sends to the trap") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } srv := &pocker.Server{ Config: cfg, Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard extensions Extensions: []pocker.Extension{ mailrelay.New(mailrelay.Config{ Domain: "mail.localhost", Upstream: mailrelay.SMTPUpstream{Addr: inbox.SMTPAddr}, }), }, // local testing: every instance gets superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" SetupApp: func(_ pocker.Instance, app core.App) error { return devusers.Ensure(app) }, } if err := srv.Run(ctx); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Mail Relay
heading: How it works
text: The extension binds PocketBase's OnMailerSend on every instance, last, after the app's own hooks. No core change. When SMTP is off it doesn't call e.Next() , so PocketBase's sendmail fallback never runs. It relays the message in-process instead. Nothing is written to the instance's settings. A backup restored somewhere else has no relay credentials in it, and falls back to stock PocketBase behavior. For each message: Check it's allowed. May this instance send ( send )? Are there no more than 5 recipients (To + Cc + Bcc)? Is the encoded size no more than 1 MiB? Count it. Each message counts once against the instance's limits, however many recipients it has. The day resets at midnight UTC. Counts are kept in memory. Set the sender. The From address becomes @ . The display name is kept, minus anything that looks like an address or a link. The app's own sender address becomes Reply-To , unless it's PocketBase's @example.com placeholder. Build and send. Bcc stays out of the headers. An X-Pocker-Instance header is added, then the message goes to the Upstream . Log it to the app's log.

title: Mail Relay
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Mail Trap
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A development mail catcher (like MailDev or Mailpit) for testing an extension or app that sends mail. In dev mode, an app whose SMTP is off sends its mail here instead of the host's sendmail , and you read it at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mail Trap
heading: Install
text: Mail Trap is built into pocketone , for a single app and for every pocker instance on a multisite host. There's nothing to install: run pocketone serve --dev with SMTP off and it's active. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() mailtrap.MustRegister(app) app.Start() Under Pocker, add mailtrap.New() to the extensions. The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap .

title: Mail Trap
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section or settings screen. It turns itself on only when both are true: the app is in dev mode ( serve --dev , or a dev instance under Pocker), and the app's SMTP is off (Settings → Mail). Turn SMTP on, or run without --dev , and it does nothing. Two environment variables move its ports: P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP 127.0.0.1:8025 (the web inbox) P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP 127.0.0.1:1025 (SMTP) Never expose these ports: anyone who can reach them can read the mail.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Use
text: Start the app with --dev . It prints the inbox address once it's active. Make your extension or app send mail: a verification, a password reset, $app.newMailClient() , a bulk mail campaign. Each caught message is also printed as one line in the terminal. Open http://127.0.0.1:8025. The list refreshes every 2 seconds. Click a message to see it as HTML , Text or Raw source. Clear empties the inbox. It keeps the last 500 messages, in memory only; they're gone when the process exits. If its ports are taken, it still catches mail and prints each message in the terminal.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Works with
text: Contracts Provides mail.fallback/v1 : with SMTP off, an app's mail goes to the contract's providers in order ( providers: { mail.fallback/v1: [mailtrap, mailrelay] } ); in dev mode Mail Trap takes it, otherwise it passes it on. Pocker One inbox for every dev instance. Each message is labeled with the instance that sent it (its X-Pocker-Instance header), and the inbox filters by instance. Mail Relay Mail Relay's example uses the trap's SMTP port as its relay, so relayed mail goes through the real SMTP path and lands here. Bulk Mail In dev mode with SMTP off, campaign mail lands in the inbox instead of being sent.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Building on Mail Trap
text: Its hook runs last. It binds OnMailerSend after the app's own hooks, so your onMailerSend hooks still run and can change the message first. When it takes a message it never calls the next handler, so sendmail never runs. SMTP for other tools. The SMTP listener accepts any message (and any AUTH), so anything that speaks SMTP can send to it. Go API. mailtrap.Default(reason) returns the process-wide trap, starting it on first use. A Trap has Messages() , Clear() , Add(from, to, raw, label) and AddMessage(msg, label) , and Handler() serves the inbox. Trap{SMTPAddr, HTTPAddr}.Start(ctx) runs a separate trap, for example in a test. Inbox API. GET /api/messages (newest first, without bodies), GET /api/messages/{id} , GET /api/messages/{id}/raw (.eml) and DELETE /api/messages , on the inbox address.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app in dev mode with the trap. Run go run ./example serve --dev from this folder, request a password reset for user@example.com (password password ) from the dashboard (log in as admin@example.com / password ), and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025. // Command example runs one app in dev mode with the dev mail trap: request a password reset for user@example.com // in the dashboard and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025. // // go run ./example serve --dev package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) mailtrap.MustRegister(app) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Mail Trap
heading: How it works
text: It's built on PocketBase's own OnMailerSend hook (the same way Mail Relay takes over an instance's mail), so PocketBase is unchanged. It used to live in core ( tools/mailer/trap.go ); it moved here on 2026-11-13.

title: MCP
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A Model Context Protocol endpoint at /mcp , so an agent (Claude Code, a Claude connector, any Streamable HTTP client) can work with your app. No sidecar process. Every tool is one REST call, run as the caller. A tool call becomes a request to your app's own API, made in-process as whoever signed in. API rules, request hooks, middleware and rate limits apply because it is the REST request. MCP makes no permission decisions of its own. The whole stock API is built in as pb_ tools (records, files, auth, collections, settings, logs, crons, SQL, backups). An app that only uses the stock API needs nothing else. Your own endpoints get tools the same way: write the REST endpoint, then the tool wrapper ( $mcp.addEndpoint in pb_hooks , or AddEndpoint from Go). Every contract the app provides is there too. Its operations are tools ( restore_points , bulkmail_start , remote_status , ...), with input schemas from the contract's types, called through the contract so its superuser check, scopes and hooks apply. MCP provides the mcp/v1 contract: another MCP server can replace this one, and serves the same contract tools. Sign-in with OAuth through the OAuth server: add https:// /mcp to Claude and sign in in a browser, as a superuser or an app user. The connection stays signed in until you revoke it. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: MCP
heading: Install
text: MCP is built into pocketone and always on, with Tokens and the OAuth server for sign-in and $mcp in pb_hooks . There's nothing to install or turn on. MCP is a member of the standard set, so every PocketOne app has it: the stock binary, every Pocker instance, and your own Go build made with standard.New() . The set also registers Tokens (with its OAuth server) for sign-in and binds $mcp in pb_hooks : set := standard.New() app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"}) app.Start() Tools that pb_hooks declare before MCP registers wait for it. The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mcp .

title: MCP
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag, environment variable or settings screen for MCP. In pocketone it serves /mcp with every built-in tool, and: anyone who can sign in through the OAuth server can connect: superusers and app users of any auth collection, each with their own rights; an agent's connection doesn't expire; it lasts until you revoke it; the server's name for clients comes from Settings → Application → Application name . A Go build can change the path, the tools, the caps and the sign-in (see Go config).

title: MCP
heading: Scopes
text: MCP registers no scopes of its own. When an agent connects, the consent page offers Full access (the account's rights, like a PocketBase auth token) or Only these , with a box for each of your token scopes (scopes that only reach contract APIs under /api/_c/ , like deploy , aren't offered unless the client asks for them). The protected resource metadata lists the same scopes in scopes_supported , so a client can ask for some up front; the user can still change the ticks. A connection limited to scopes is held to them exactly like an API token with those scopes on the REST API: Each tool call is checked against the scopes' paths and methods (or Match guards). A request they don't cover is refused with 403 , and the tool returns that as an error. Collection rules see only those scopes in @request.headers.x_token_scope_ . tools/list hides tools none of the scopes reaches, and the instructions name the scopes. The token itself still works only on /mcp . To limit an agent further, sign it in as an account with fewer rights.

title: MCP
heading: Behind a proxy
text: The OAuth resource URL must match the URL clients use. MCP builds it from the request's host, taking the scheme from Settings → Application URL when its host is the same, else from TLS or X-Forwarded-Proto . If your proxy rewrites the host, set Config.PublicURL in a Go build.

title: MCP
heading: Browsers
text: Requests with an Origin header from another site get 403 . Clients that send no Origin , such as Claude's servers and Claude Code, pass. A Go build can allow more origins with Config.AllowedOrigins .

title: MCP
heading: Connect Claude Code
text: claude mcp add --transport http my-app https:// /mcp claude mcp login my-app # or /mcp in a session A browser opens on your app's sign-in page. Sign in (as an app user, or with Sign in as a superuser ), check what the consent page says and click Allow . Claude and Claude Code can connect without registering, through their published client metadata documents. For a Claude connector, add https:// /mcp as a custom connector and sign in the same way. Other MCP clients register themselves with your app first.

title: MCP
heading: Paste a token instead
text: A PocketBase auth token, or an API token not bound to any resource, works on /mcp as it does on the REST API, and tool calls forward it unchanged. A scoped API token works only if one of its scopes covers /mcp ; to limit an agent to scopes, connect it through the consent page instead (see Scopes).

title: MCP
heading: Who a tool call runs as
text: Whoever signed in. A superuser gets what the API gives superusers; an app user gets what your collection rules give them. Superuser-only tools are left out of other callers' tool list (that's presentation; the endpoint still decides).

title: MCP
heading: See and revoke connected agents
text: Each sign-in creates an API token bound to /mcp , named " (OAuth)". They're listed under Settings → API tokens with an oauth: label; click Revoke to disconnect an agent.

title: MCP
heading: Built-in tools
text: One per stock endpoint: health pb_check_health everyone records pb_list_records ( perPage 20 by default), pb_get_record , pb_create_record , pb_update_record , pb_delete_record , pb_run_batch per collection rules auth pb_list_auth_methods , pb_request_otp , pb_request_verification , pb_confirm_verification , pb_request_password_reset , pb_confirm_password_reset , pb_request_email_change , pb_confirm_email_change per collection files pb_download_file (protected files through a file token made as the caller; images as images, text as text, others as embedded data; up to 10 MB) per view rules collections pb_list_collections , pb_get_collection , pb_create_collection , pb_update_collection , pb_delete_collection , pb_truncate_collection , pb_import_collections , pb_get_collection_scaffolds , pb_list_oauth2_providers , pb_dry_run_view superusers settings pb_get_settings , pb_update_settings , pb_test_s3 , pb_test_email , pb_generate_apple_client_secret superusers logs pb_list_logs , pb_get_log , pb_get_log_stats , pb_truncate_logs superusers crons pb_list_crons , pb_run_cron superusers sql pb_run_sql superusers backups pb_list_backups , pb_create_backup , pb_upload_backup , pb_download_backup , pb_delete_backup , pb_restore_backup superusers Record create and update take field values in data , with files as {"name", "base64", "type"} objects ( "field+" appends, "field-" removes). pb_delete_collection , pb_truncate_collection , pb_delete_backup and pb_restore_backup need confirm set to the name. Endpoints that hand out a new token (auth-with- , auth-refresh, impersonate) and realtime (a stream) aren't tools. Each tool call counts against the API's rate limits, like any request. Batch sub-requests skip route middleware (PocketBase behaviour).

title: MCP
heading: Add your own tools from pb_hooks
text: Write the endpoint as you would anyway, then declare its tool at the top level of a hooks file: // pb_hooks/blog.pb.js routerAdd('POST', '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', (e) = { / … / }, $apis.requireSuperuserAuth()) $mcp.addEndpoint({ name: 'blog_publish_post', description: 'Publish a draft post and email subscribers.', method: 'POST', path: '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', // {id} comes from args.id inputSchema: { type: 'object', required: ['id'], properties: { id: { type: 'string' } } }, // optional; request is the default mapping, return a changed copy request: ({ args, auth, request }) = ({ ...request, body: { at: args.when } }), // optional; throw for an error the model can read response: ({ status, json }) = (status === 200 ? { published: json.id } : json), }) $mcp.instructions('blog_publish_post also emails subscribers.') The tool runs the request as the caller, so the route's own auth check is what protects it. One tool serves every caller. title , outputSchema and annotations are optional. Without annotations, GET tools are marked read-only and DELETE tools destructive. request gets {args, auth, request} and returns {method, path, query, body, headers, files} (missing keys keep the default; $mcp.pathValue(v) escapes a path segment). response gets {args, auth, status, headers, body, json, truncated} . Both run one at a time on the VM that loaded the hooks and may use the file's top-level variables; the REST call itself runs outside it. Keep them small: the work belongs in the endpoint. $mcp.tools() lists the registered tool names. Agents are told to prefer the app's own tools: when an app has any, the instructions sent on connect say to use them when one fits and fall back to pb_ , and the tool list shows them first. Put work that spans collections in a custom endpoint (one transaction, the app's checks), not in a chain of pb_ calls. A wrapper can sit over a stock endpoint too, to give it the app's meaning (for example notes_add_note over POST /api/collections/notes/records ).

title: MCP
heading: In the logs
text: Without the OAuth server on the app, MCP logs a warning on serve: mcp: the OAuth server (ext/tokens) is off; /mcp accepts pasted PocketBase auth tokens only, and clients can't sign in by themselves . In pocketone it always is.

title: MCP
heading: Works with
text: OAuth (in Tokens) Signs MCP clients in. MCP points clients at it from the protected resource metadata, turns on its client self-registration, and makes tokens bound to /mcp never expire. Who may sign in comes from its Collections (default: superusers and every auth collection). Tokens The access tokens are API tokens bound to https:// /mcp (RFC 8707): they work nowhere else, and are listed and revoked under Settings → API tokens. Your token scopes On a full-access connection a tool call holds every scope you registered (except ones its collection can't hold): $tokens.requireScope guards pass, and @request.headers.x_token_scope_ is "1" in collection rules. On a connection limited to scopes it holds only those, and requests they don't cover are refused (see Scopes). Pages A pb_pages +api.js route is a REST endpoint like any other; declare its tool with $mcp.addEndpoint . S3 Redirect pb_download_file follows its one redirect to storage. JS hooks $mcp in pb_hooks (above). Under Pocker, every instance gets MCP from the standard set, with its own tokens, OAuth sign-in and /mcp ; an instance turns it off with extensions.mcp.enabled: false .

title: MCP
heading: Tools from Go
text: An extension registered on the same app reaches the server with mcp.For(app) : server := mcp.For(app) // or the mcp.Server that mcp.MustRegister returned // the endpoint, as you'd write it anyway app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.POST("/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish", publish).Bind(apis.RequireSuperuserAuth()) return se.Next() }) // the tool wrapper server.MustAddEndpoint(mcp.Endpoint{ Name: "blog_publish_post", // lowercase _ _ ; pb_ is the built-ins' Title: "Publish post", Description: "Publish a draft post and email subscribers.", Method: http.MethodPost, Path: "/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish", // {id} is filled from args.id InputSchema: map[string]any{"type": "object", "required": []any{"id"}, "properties": map[string]any{"id": map[string]any{"type": "string"}}}, Annotations: mcp.Write, // default from the method: GET read-only, DELETE destructive Request: nil, // optional: func(c mcp.Call) ( mcp.Request, error) Response: nil, // optional: func(c mcp.Call, res mcp.Response) (any, error) }) server.AddInstructions("blog_publish_post also emails subscribers.") The default mapping: {name} path segments come from the argument of the same name, escaped. Empty, . and .. are refused (the router would clean them into another route). Other arguments go to the query string for GET , HEAD and DELETE , and to the JSON body for other methods. An argument holding a file, {"name": "a.png", "base64": "…", "type": "image/png"} or a list of them, makes the body multipart (other arguments ride along as @jsonPayload ), the way PocketBase takes uploads. Up to 10 MB per file. Arguments are checked against the schema's required , top-level type s, enum s and additionalProperties: false before the request is made; the endpoint validates the rest. The result: 2xx JSON comes back as the result (also as structuredContent when it's an object); other 2xx bodies as text; 4xx/5xx as a tool error with PocketBase's {status, message, data} , so the model can fix its call. JSON results are capped at 1 MB and say when they were cut. Request sees the caller ( c.Auth() ) but can't change who the request runs as: an Authorization header it sets is dropped. Build paths with c.Path(template) or mcp.PathValue , never by joining raw strings. c.Do makes another request as the same caller (e.g. a file token before a download). Response may return any JSON-able value, a string, or an mcp.Content list (images, text, embedded files). SuperuserOnly: true hides a tool from other callers' tool list.

title: MCP
heading: Tools from an extension
text: An extension's API is contracts, and a contract's operations are already tools: nothing to add. For a tool that isn't a contract operation, an extension calls mcpv1.AddTool(app, mcpv1.Tool{...}) (and mcpv1.AddInstructions ) in its Register , which works with whichever extension provides mcp/v1. A PocketOne extension that adds tools names them _ _ : its name (with - as _ ), then at least two lowercase words, such as notes_list_notes or oauth_server_revoke_client . Each has a description, and an input schema, when it has one, is a JSON Schema object. The conformance test checks all of this when the extension's test puts an MCP server on the test apps: conformance.Run(t, newExtension, conformance.Options{Setup: func(app core.App) error { _, err := mcp.Register(app, mcp.Config{}) return err }})

title: MCP
heading: How sign-in works
text: With Tokens (with its OAuth server) on the app, /mcp uses OAuth the way Claude connectors and Claude Code expect: A request without a token gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https:// /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp" . The protected resource metadata names the app as its authorization server (the OAuth server's issuer). The OAuth server publishes the authorization server metadata, with PKCE S256, client metadata documents and dynamic registration. The client registers itself (Claude's published identity through a client metadata document, or dynamic registration), and the user signs in in a browser. The access token is an API token bound to https:// /mcp . It carries the account's rights but works only on /mcp . Each MCP request makes a PocketBase auth token for the same account, and tool calls reach the REST API with it (as Pages' ctx.pb() does). For a token limited to scopes, those requests carry the scopes ( tokensv1.WithScopes , through the tokens/v1 contract), and Tokens checks them as it would a scoped token's request. Without the OAuth server, /mcp falls back to PocketBaseTokenAuth : pasted PocketBase auth tokens ( Collections limits which auth collections, default any), and the warning above. Config.Auth overrides the choice; mcp.OAuth{Issuer} overrides the authorization server listed in the metadata.

title: MCP
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with an MCP endpoint at /mcp : the built-in pb_ tools, a tool over a Go route and one over a JS route. cd example go run . serve The example registers devusers, so the logins are admin@example.com / password (superuser) and user@example.com / password (user). It also registers Tokens (with its OAuth server) for OAuth sign-in, and adds a tool over a Go route ( example_get_whoami ) and one over a JS route ( example_list_recent_users , in pb_hooks/mcp.pb.js ). Then: claude mcp add --transport http pb-example http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp claude mcp login pb-example // Command example runs one PocketOne app with an MCP endpoint at /mcp: the built-in pb_ tools (the whole stock REST // API), a tool over a Go route, and a tool over a JS route from pb_hooks/mcp.pb.js. // // cd ext/mcp/example && go run . serve // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. // // Sign-in is OAuth (the OAuth server in ext/tokens): add the endpoint to Claude Code and sign in in the browser when it // asks. Tool calls run as whoever signed in. // // claude mcp add --transport http pb-example http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp // claude mcp login pb-example (or /mcp in a session) package main import ( "log" "net/http" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit/js" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mcp" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" // OAuth sign-in: API tokens + the authorization server. ext/mcp picks it up on serve and turns on dynamic client // registration. tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) // its OAuth server comes with it server := mcp.MustRegister(app, mcp.Config{ Name: "pb-example", Description: "Example PocketOne app with ext/mcp.", }) // A tool from Go: write the REST endpoint, then the tool wrapper. The tool runs the request as the caller, so // the route's own auth check is what protects it. app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.GET("/api/example/whoami", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"collection": e.Auth.Collection().Name, "email": e.Auth.Email()}) }).Bind(apis.RequireAuth()) return se.Next() }) server.MustAddEndpoint(mcp.Endpoint{ Name: "example_get_whoami", Title: "Who am I", Description: "The signed-in record's collection and email.", Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/api/example/whoami", }) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { mcp.BindJS(app, rt) }, }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

text: Name , Version , Description , Icons app name slug, dev serverInfo Instructions generated first paragraph of the instructions sent on connect PublicURL the request's host origin used for the OAuth resource URL; set it when a proxy rewrites the host Auth OAuth{} with Tokens' OAuth server on, else PocketBaseTokenAuth{} the Authenticator BuiltinGroups all which pb_ groups ( mcp.BuiltinGroups ) ReadOnlyBuiltins false keep only the read-only pb_ tools NoBuiltins false drop every pb_ tool MaxResponse 1 MB cap on a JSON result MaxFile 10 MB cap on one file uploaded or downloaded through a tool AllowedOrigins none extra browser origins allowed besides the app's own The endpoint speaks MCP Streamable HTTP, stateless: each POST carries one JSON-RPC message and gets JSON back. Protocol versions 2025-11-25 , 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26 . Tools only for now.

title: Mothership
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A control plane for a fleet of edges. The mothership is a PocketOne app that records which edges exist and which instances run where. Each edge follows it, serves its own instances and forwards requests for the rest to the edge that runs them. One operator, no users: owners and accounts are the tenants extension (planned), which extends the mothership through its collections and the mirror's extensions. Each layer is optional: an edge runs without a mothership, and a mothership without tenants. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mothership
heading: Install
text: The edge side (the mirror package) is built into pocketone . It turns on when pocketone.yaml names a provider and has a mothership section (below); pocketone serve then takes its instances and the other edges from the mothership. The mothership side has no switch yet. In the Go code of the PocketOne app that will be the mothership, create its collections once the app has bootstrapped: if err := mothership.EnsureCollections(app); err != nil { return err } The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mothership . In your own edge build, mirror.FromSection(log) returns the mirror for the config (nil without a mothership section); use it as the host's instance source and the router's edge source, as examples/pocketone/multi.go does.

title: Mothership
heading: Configure
text: On each edge, add a mothership section to the host's config; the mirror becomes the host's instance.source/v1. Logins come from the private .env : multisite: {} mothership: url: http://10.88.0.10:8090 email: $MOTHERSHIP_EMAIL password: $MOTHERSHIP_PASSWORD self: lax-1 # this edge's edge_id (or edges.self) internal_url: http://10.88.0.5:8080 region: lax apex: example.com # .example.com routes to each instance url and self are required. The edge logs in as a superuser of the mothership. On the mothership, there's nothing to configure beyond creating the collections.

title: Mothership
heading: mothership:
text: A community mothership to mirror instances and edges from: url, login, this edge's id, internal URL, region, apex. url string The mothership's URL. Required. email string Superuser email this edge logs in with; use a $VAR from the .env. password string Superuser password; use a $VAR from the .env. self string This edge's edge_id, such as lax-1. Default: the edges section's self. Required. internal_url string Where other edges reach this one. Set: the edge registers itself when the mothership has no record for it. region string Region recorded when the edge registers itself. apex string Makes . a hostname of every instance. Empty: hosts only. heartbeat duration How often this edge marks itself online. Default 15s; negative: never. resync duration How often everything is reloaded, in case a change was missed. Default 10m.

title: Mothership
heading: Use
text: You manage the fleet in the mothership's dashboard, in two collections only superusers can read or write: edges : edge_id (such as lax-1 ), internal_url , region , status ( online , draining , offline ) and last_seen . An edge with internal_url set registers itself when it has no record, marks itself online every 15 s, and offline when it shuts down. instances : name ( . routes to it), hosts (extra hostnames), edge (where it runs), power (off answers 409 "instance is powered off"), suspension (non-empty answers 403 with that message), dev , version , secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , plugins (extension settings; the field keeps its old name) and status . Changes reach the edges within moments over PocketBase's realtime stream; there's no polling. To move an instance, change its edge : the old edge drops its full record and forwards to the new one until the new edge has it. An instance with no edge isn't served anywhere.

title: Mothership
heading: Works with
text: Multisite The mirror is the host's instance source: which instances exist and which this edge runs. Edge The mirror is also an edge source: where the other edges are, so requests for their instances are forwarded. It combines with a fixed edges list. Docker and Pocker Run the instances this edge owns, with the version, secrets, limits and extension settings from each record. Tenants (planned) Adds owners and accounts through mirror extensions.

title: Mothership
heading: Building on Mothership
text: Your own fields and collections. EnsureCollections leaves fields an extension added alone, so an extension can add its own fields and collections to the mothership. Mirror extensions. Pass a mirror.Extension to mirror.FromSection or mirror.Config.Extensions . Views() adds filtered subscriptions (such as owners filtered to instances_via_owner.edge ?= {edge} ), Instance() adjusts each instance as it's built (block a suspended owner's instances, add an owner's trusted IPs), and Changed() names the instances a change in its views affects. Go API. mirror.New(mirror.Config{...}) builds a mirror without the config file. Get(view, id) and Records(view) read any view; SelfRecord() is this edge's record id.

title: Mothership
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go yet. The stock binary's multi-instance mode, examples/pocketone/multi.go , follows a mothership when the config has the section.

title: Mothership
heading: How it works
text: Each edge subscribes to filtered views, so it only receives what concerns it: edges edges all forwarding, and health from heartbeats routes instances fields id,name,hosts,edge,updated the routing table: any edge may get any visitor local instances edge = full records (secrets, limits, plugins) for instances this edge runs An instance moving away shows up in routes and its full record is dropped; one moving here arrives in local . The stream reconnects and reloads on its own, and reloads everything every 10 minutes in case anything was missed. Filters cut what each edge downloads and keeps (most edges run a few of thousands of instances). They are not a security boundary while edges log in as superusers.

title: Mothership
heading: Status
text: Early. Built: the edges and instances collections ( EnsureCollections ) and the edge side ( mirror ). Not yet: the mothership's own endpoints (placement, moves) and instance status reports.

heading: License
text: MIT

title: Multisite
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Many PocketOne instances behind one listener, routed by hostname. Each request's hostname picks an instance, the request passes the gates (such as the firewall), and a runtime serves it: pocker runs instances in-process, docker runs each in its own container, and a host can run both. Everything a host plugs in is a host-scope contract: runtime/v1, gate/v1, tls/v1, http.wrap/v1 and instance.source/v1. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Multisite
heading: Install
text: Multisite is built into pocketone . It takes over serve when pocketone.yaml has a multisite section; without one, pocketone serve runs a single app as usual. multisite: {} providers: runtime/v1: [pocker, docker] # optional: which runtimes, in preference order (default: every configured one) In your own Go build, pass the host extensions you link (runtimes in preference order), build the host from the config and run it. examples/pocketone/multi.go is the stock binary's version: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Choices: providersSection, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{servertiming.New(), autotls.New(), &pocker.Provider{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath}}}) if errors.Is(err, multisite.ErrNoProvider) { // no multisite section in pocketone.yaml: serve a single app instead } err = h.Run(ctx) At startup the host logs who provides each host contract, e.g. multisite: runtime/v1 ← pocker, docker . The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/multisite .

title: Multisite
heading: Configure
text: A host reads these pocketone.yaml sections: multisite: {} # host mode server: https: ":443" # the main address http: ":80" # redirects to https (alone: serves plain HTTP) plain: [":8080"] # extra plain-HTTP addresses, no redirect (e.g. a private network) tls: { cert: cert.pem, key: key.pem } # reloaded when the files change; or the autotls section instances: file: ./instances.yaml # where the instances come from dev: false # also serve unknown hostnames pocker: { root: ./pb_root } # a runtime's own section (pocker; docker only runs with its section) firewall: { allow_cidrs: [10.0.0.0/8] } # any gate's section turns that gate on server belongs to Config; providers is the contracts' section. With no https or http , the host listens on 127.0.0.1:8090 . The instances section is this extension's (keys below). In production the instances file is required; with dev: true it's optional. The app section is for a single app and is refused on a multisite host: each instance has its own folder under its runtime's root.

title: Multisite
heading: instances:
text: Where a multi-instance host's instances come from (a YAML file), and dev mode (serve unknown hostnames). file string instances.yaml The instances file (id, hosts and settings for each instance), reloaded when it changes. dev bool Also serve unknown hostnames: each becomes an instance named after it, in dev mode, with its folder made on first use.

title: Multisite
heading: multisite:
text: Serve many instances (a multisite host) instead of a single app. The runtimes are the providers of runtime/v1.

title: Multisite
heading: The instances file
text: instances: id: blog # also the folder name: /blog hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com] id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... } # the app's environment, seen by its JS hooks encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # encrypts the app's stored settings access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] } limits: { max_js_execution: 60s } # over the runtime's defaults extensions: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } } # settings for extensions, by name id: old hosts: [old.example.com] blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" } The file is checked for changes every 2 seconds; edits apply without restarting the host. Ids are lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes. Other fields: version and runtime (which release or runtime runs it), dir (another folder), dev , superusers (pocker upserts them when the app starts), private (for host Go code, never seen by JS) and remote (another server runs it).

title: Multisite
heading: What a request gets
text: A hostname no instance maps gets 404, and no folder is created. In dev mode it becomes a new instance named after the hostname, in dev mode. A blocked instance answers every request with its status and message. An instance with remote set is forwarded there after the gates (a plain proxy to the URL, or Edge for a fleet). Contracts the host provides for its instances (docker's remote/v1) answer after the gates and the blocked check, so the firewall, rate limits and a powered-off answer apply to them too. GET /.well-known/health on any hostname reports the host's status, how many instances it knows and how many are running.

title: Multisite
heading: Switching runtime
text: Switching between pocker and docker is a config change ( providers: { runtime/v1: [docker] } , or an instance's own runtime: docker ): both keep instances in / . Stop the containers first when leaving docker (they keep running across a host restart on purpose). Data only moves forward: an instance started on a newer version than wrote its data is upgraded.

title: Multisite
heading: Works with
text: Pocker runtime/v1: every instance runs in this process. Docker runtime/v1: each instance runs in its own container (with a docker section). Firewall A gate: peer allow-list, client IPs and rate limits. On when the config has firewall or rate_limits . Edge Forwards requests for instances another edge runs (the edges section). Mothership Its mirror is instance.source/v1 instead of the instances file, and lists the other edges. Auto TLS Certificates for the main listener, issued for the hostnames instances map. Stats Measures disk use and last request for each instance. Server Timing Server-Timing headers for each step of a request.

title: Multisite
heading: Building on Host
text: Host extensions. A multisite.Extension ( Name , RegisterHost(h) ) provides host-scope contracts on h.Scope : a runtime ( runtimev1.Contract.ProvideIn(h.Scope, rt) ), a gate, TLS, a wrapper, an instance source. It provides nothing when it isn't configured (no section). Pass it in Options.Extensions , or multisite.Link it from an init so linking the package is enough (the firewall does). By hand: h.Use(exts...) , then h.Setup(choices) . Runtime. runtimev1.Runtime ( Name , Serves , ServeInstance , Ready ), with optional Prechecker , Syncer , Starter , Statser and Shutdowner . Each instance runs on the runtime it names, else the first that serves it. Instance source. sourcev1.Source ( Snapshot , Watch ) feeds instances from anywhere, such as a control plane. The instances file ( YAMLSource ) is the default and steps aside for any other provider. Gates. A gatev1.Gate checks the peer ( AllowPeer ) and admits each request ( Admit ); ClientIPResolver passes the real client IP on to the app. Gates set on h.Gates directly run after the contract's. Forwarding. multisite.Options.Forward serves requests for instances with remote set (Edge fills it). Instance routes. Host.InstanceRoutes wrap the runtime for instances this host runs: they run after the peer check, the blocked answer and the gates, and before the runtime (never for forwarded instances). multisite.InstanceOf(r) is the resolved instance and multisite.InstanceID fits extkit's host handlers, so a contract the host provides for its instances goes here: remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(h.Scope, myRemote) h.InstanceRoutes = append(h.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return remotev1.W.HostHandler(h.Scope, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next) }) Listeners and wrappers. tls/v1 (or Host.TLS ) sets the listener's TLS, http.wrap/v1 providers wrap the whole handler (outside Host.Wrappers ), and Host.Background runs jobs until shutdown. Per-instance settings. An extension reads its own extensions. with inst.ExtensionConfig(name) and multisite.DecodeExtensionConfig .

title: Multisite
heading: Example
text: A toy host: instances from a YAML file, served by a runtime that answers with the instance it resolved. Run it from this folder with go run ./example --instances instances.yaml , then curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' localhost:8090/ . // A minimal host: instances from a YAML file, routed by hostname, served by a toy runtime that answers with the // instance it resolved. Real hosts plug in a provider instead (ext/pocker in-process, ext/docker in containers). // // go run ./example --instances instances.yaml // curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' localhost:8090/ package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "net/http" "os" "os/signal" "syscall" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/multisite" ) type echoRuntime struct{} func (echoRuntime) Name() string { return "echo" } func (echoRuntime) Serves(inst multisite.Instance) bool { return true } func (echoRuntime) Ready() bool { return true } func (echoRuntime) ServeInstance(w http.ResponseWriter, r http.Request, inst multisite.Instance) { fmt.Fprintf(w, "instance %s (%s%s)\n", inst.ID, r.Host, r.URL.Path) } func main() { instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file: instances: [{id: blog, hosts: [blog.localhost]}]") listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address") flag.Parse() ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() h := &multisite.Host{Source: &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: instances}, Runtimes: []multisite.Runtime{echoRuntime{}}, Listeners: multisite.Listeners{Listen: listen}} if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit(1) } }

title: Multisite
heading: How it works
text: Instance , InstanceSource , YAMLSource The instance record (instance.source/v1) and where instances come from. Directory Instances by hostname and id, kept current from the source. Handler Health path, peer check, hostname, blocked, then remote (the Forward hook) or local (the instance routes, then the runtime), with the gates. Runtime runtime/v1: what runs instances. One or more per host, in preference order. Gate , ChainGates , HostGate Request gates (gate/v1). Extension , Link , Host.Use , Host.Setup Host extensions and the host's contract scope. Serve , TLSProvider Listeners: plain, TLS (a provider such as autotls, or cert files reloaded on change), redirect, graceful shutdown. Host , FromConfig All of the above assembled, by hand or from pocketone.yaml .
