text: MIT

title: Pocker
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Many PocketOne instances in one process (like Docker, but for PocketOne), routed by hostname. Each instance is a normal app folder and starts on its first request, in tens of milliseconds. Pocker provides runtime/v1 for Multisite; its peer Docker runs each instance in a container instead. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Pocker
heading: Install
text: Pocker is built into pocketone . Add a multisite section to pocketone.yaml and pocketone serve hosts many instances instead of one app, with pocker as the runtime (docker too, when it has its docker section): multisite: {} In your own Go build, add it to the host's extensions ( examples/pocketone/multi.go is the stock binary's version), or run a pocker.Server on its own as the example does: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{ &pocker.Provider{ Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard set (tokens, mcp, pitr, ...) Extensions: []pocker.Extension{ myextension.New(), // your own PocketOne extensions, on every instance too }, }, }}) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pocker .

title: Pocker
heading: Configure
text: The pocker section sets where instances live, the JS pool, outbound network and the default limits for every instance (keys below). Listeners, instances and the firewall are the Multisite sections ( server , instances , firewall ). multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } pocker: root: ./pb_root # one folder per instance: / hooks_pool_size: 2 egress_allow: [] # private networks instances may still reach max_js_execution: 30s # default limits; each instance can override them max_js_allocation: 64MiB An instance overrides any limit in its own limits (missing fields keep the default): instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] limits: { max_js_execution: 60s, max_concurrent_js: 32 } Every instance runs the PocketOne code in the binary; an instance's version is ignored.

title: Pocker
heading: pocker:
text: Runtime provider pocker: instances run in-process (root folder, hooks pool, egress allow list, instance limit defaults). root string ./pb_root The folder holding one folder per instance: / . hooks_pool_size int 2 Ignored: each instance has one JS VM (ext/jsvm). Kept so existing configs load. max_js_execution duration 30s Longest any single JS call (hook, route, cron job, migration) may run. max_js_allocation int 67108864 Largest result a JS built-in may allocate in one step, such as 64MiB. max_call_stack_size int 2000 Deepest JS recursion allowed. max_sleep duration 10s Longest a JS sleep() call may wait. max_query_duration duration 30s Longest an SQL statement without its own deadline may run. http_send_max_timeout duration 1m0s Longest timeout a JS $http.send call may use. http_send_max_body int 10485760 Largest response body a JS $http.send call may read, such as 10MiB. max_concurrent_js int 16 JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail. egress_allow list of string Private networks (CIDRs) instances may still connect to. Default none: public addresses only.

title: Pocker
heading: Try it with any hostname
text: # pocketone.yaml server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" } multisite: {} instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } pocketone serve curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost In dev mode a hostname no instance maps becomes an instance named after it, its folder is made on first use, and it runs in dev mode. In production only the hostnames in the instances file are served (see Multisite).

title: Pocker
heading: Each instance
text: A normal app folder, / : pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_public . Its dashboard is at https:// /_/ . Its JS hooks see only its own secrets , through $os.getenv and process.env . A change to its secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , dev , dir , superusers , private , extensions or remote restarts it if it's running (the app stops, then a fresh one starts, as in a process restart). A hostname change doesn't restart it. A change in pb_hooks restarts just that instance. A broken hooks file affects only that instance (below).

title: Pocker
heading: Broken hook files
text: In dev mode, a pb_hooks file that fails to load is logged and skipped, and the rest of the instance runs, so you can fix it live. Otherwise an instance doesn't start with a broken file. When a running instance's pb_hooks change, Pocker restarts it as PocketBase's watcher restarts a process: the running app stops (requests in flight are cut off), then a fresh app starts with the new files. Only one app has an instance's folder open at a time, so migrations and bootstrap code never run beside a live app. A broken file in production leaves the instance down: requests get 502 with the error, which also goes to the instance log, and the first request after a fix starts it.

title: Pocker
heading: Logs
text: The app's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance, in its pb_data . console. from JS hooks goes to /logs/exec.log as JSON lines ( message , stream , time ), rotated to exec.log.1 at 10 MiB. A start failure is written there too.

title: Pocker
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Routing, listeners, instances file and gates. Pocker is one of its runtimes (runtime/v1). Sandbox Every instance's JS hooks, SQL and outbound network run in it, so one instance can't reach another or the host. Firewall Peer allow-list and rate limits in front of every instance; per-instance limits in extensions.firewall . Auto TLS In the stock binary: certificates for the hostnames instances map ( autotls section). Server Timing In the stock binary: Server-Timing headers on every response. Mailtrap In the stock binary: dev instances with SMTP off send mail to a local inbox. Edge Instances another edge runs are forwarded there instead of started here. Stats Measures disk use and last request for each instance under root . PocketOne extensions In your own build, any extension such as PITR, S3 Fallback or Mail Relay runs on every instance, and an instance's extensions. settings override the extension's defaults. enabled: false turns it off for that instance.

title: Pocker
heading: Building on Pocker
text: Standard set (required). pocker.Provider.Standard (or pocker.Server.Standard , ManagerOptions.Standard ) is ext/standard's set, and Pocker won't start an instance without it: a server without one refuses to run, so no host can make an instance that lacks the standard extensions. Every instance gets its members, each turned off per instance with extensions. .enabled: false , and its startup lines ( standard: on: ... ) are in the instance's own log. Listing a member in Extensions too is an error. Contracts the host provides. Server.Host (or Provider.Host ) is the host's contract scope. A contract the host provides for its instances steps aside inside each instance's app, and the host answers it on the instance's hostname in Server.InstanceRoutes (or Provider.InstanceRoutes , ManagerOptions.InstanceRoutes ): after the gates and the blocked answer, before the app. pocker.Remote(m, host) is remote/v1 for Pocker instances (restart through the Manager, logs from logs/exec.log ); add your own auth: host := extkit.NewScope("multisite") srv.Host = host srv.OnStart = func(m pocker.Manager) { remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(host, pocker.Remote(m, host)) } srv.InstanceRoutes = append(srv.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return remotev1.W.HostHandler(host, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next) }) deploy/v1 works the same way with deploy.New(...) as the handler: deployv1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(host, ...) and extkit.HostRoutes(host, deployv1.Contract, multisite.InstanceID, next) as an instance route. Extensions. pocker.Provider.Extensions (or pocker.Server.Extensions ) takes any extkit.Extension , registered on each instance's app before it starts with that instance's extensions. settings. Host-level code can implement AppIniter , JSIniter , Starter , or be a host extension ( multisite.Extension , registered on the host like any other: servertiming, autotls). See POCKER.md. Setup per instance. SetupApp(inst, app) runs after migrations and before the app serves, e.g. to add a route checked against inst.Private . Manager. OnStart hands host code the Manager : WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn) changes an instance's files while it's stopped (deploys, restores), StartInstance , Running , InstanceDir , LogInstance . Restarts. app.Restart() (a backup restore, PITR) restarts only that instance.

title: Pocker
heading: Example
text: A Pocker build with one extension: a Go route and an admin dashboard page on every instance, in dev mode. Run it from this folder with go run ./example , then open http://blog.localhost:8090/_/ (login admin@example.com / password ). // Command pocker-extension is a Pocker build with one extension: a Go route and an admin dashboard page, // added to every instance. See docs/extensions.md. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "context" "embed" "io/fs" "log" "net/http" "os" "os/signal" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pocker" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/standard" ) //go:embed ui var uiFiles embed.FS func main() { cfg := pocker.DefaultConfig() cfg.Dev = true // any hostname; drop this for production (instances.yaml required) ui, _ := fs.Sub(uiFiles, "ui") srv := &pocker.Server{ Config: cfg, Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard extensions (tokens, mcp, pages, pitr, ...) // Runs for every instance's app after its migrations, before it serves. SetupApp: func(inst pocker.Instance, app core.App) error { // local testing: every instance gets superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" if err := devusers.Ensure(app); err != nil { return err } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { // a Go route, superuser only se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]string{"instance": inst.ID}) }).Bind(apis.RequireSuperuserAuth()) // an admin dashboard extension: ui/main.js is loaded by the dashboard before its router starts se.UIExtensions = append(se.UIExtensions, core.UIExtension{Name: "hello", FS: ui}) return se.Next() }) return nil }, } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt) defer stop() if err := srv.Run(ctx); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Pocker
heading: Untrusted instances
text: Pocker runs every instance's JS hooks in the sandbox. For why that's safe enough to host code from people you don't know, and where it isn't, see How is this safe?. Memory is the main limit: only one-shot allocations are capped, so a hook that grows memory slowly affects the whole process. POCKER.md lists what the sandbox covers.

title: Pocker
heading: Reference
text: POCKER.md is the full guide: production pocketone.yaml , every instance field, extension interfaces, the sandbox, PocketBase changes and versions.

title: Pocker
text: Pocker hosts many PocketOne instances in one process. It is PocketOne itself (this repo tracks upstream PocketBase and shares its history) plus a small engine in this folder, run by the stock pocketone binary as a runtime/v1 provider (a multisite section in pocketone.yaml). One port, many instances. Each request's hostname maps to a canonical instance id. Each instance is a normal app folder, / ( pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_public ), with its own environment for JS hooks ( $os.getenv , process.env ), its own JS migrations and its own settings encryption key. An instance's app starts on its first request (tens of milliseconds) and keeps running.

title: Pocker
heading: Dev mode: any hostname
text: # pocketone.yaml server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" } multisite: {} instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } pocketone serve curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost A hostname the instance source doesn't map uses the hostname itself as its id (lowercase, no port, no trailing dot; anything that isn't a safe folder name gets 400), its folder is created on first use, and apps run in dev mode. The instances file (or another source) is optional in dev mode; hosts it maps keep their own ids.

title: Pocker
heading: Production: mapped hostnames only
text: Without dev mode, Pocker serves only what an instance source maps. The built-in source is the instances section's YAML file (reloaded when it changes; the host refuses to start without it): # instances.yaml instances: id: blog # folder /blog hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com] id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... } # the app's environment encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # encrypts the app's stored settings; not visible to JS access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] } extensions: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } } # settings for extensions, by name id: old hosts: [old.example.com] blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" } Unknown hosts get 404 and no folder is ever created from a request. Ids are lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes. Pocker runs whatever instances the host's instance.source/v1 provider supplies, and nothing else: the file by default. Hosting platforms provide that contract themselves instead (for example a control plane streaming the hostname - id map over SSE); a community mothership is one (the mothership section, ext/mothership). Tests provide it with sourcetest. pocketone.yaml for a production host (each extension owns its section; every field has a default): server: https: ":443" http: ":80" # redirects to HTTPS (and answers ACME HTTP-01 challenges) plain: [] # extra plain-HTTP listeners (no TLS, no redirect), e.g. a private network other servers forward on tls: { cert: /path/fullchain.pem, key: /path/privkey.pem } # re-read when they change; or the autotls section multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } pocker: root: ./pb_root hooks_pool_size: 2 egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach (default none) # default limits for every instance (each instance can override them, see below) max_js_execution: 30s # any single JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) max_js_allocation: 64MiB # one-shot JS allocations max_call_stack_size: 2000 max_sleep: 10s max_query_duration: 30s # any SQL statement without its own deadline http_send_max_timeout: 60s http_send_max_body: 10MiB max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail rate_limits: # per client IP and per instance; trusted clients get the trusted set ip_hourly: 1000 instance_hourly: 10000 ip_concurrent: 15 instance_concurrent: 250 file_weight: 0.1 # a /api/files request costs a tenth trusted: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_hourly: 20000, ip_concurrent: 50, instance_concurrent: 250 } # off: true # no rate limiting (the default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set) firewall: allow_cidrs: [] # peers allowed to connect (empty = everyone); others get 403 trusted_proxies: [] # peers whose client-IP headers are believed client_ip_headers: [CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP] trusted_clients: [] # client IPs with the trusted limits on every instance trusted_client_headers: [X-Client-IP] # a trusted client names its end user (own buckets) rate_limit_header_prefix: X-RateLimit # autotls: # automatic certificates (ACME, via CertMagic, Caddy's certificate engine) # auto: true # email: ops@example.com # ca: letsencrypt # letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL # storage: ./pb_root/.pocker-certs # domains: [" .example.com", "example.com"] # obtained up front; wildcards need dns # dns: { provider: cloudflare, api_token_env: CF_API_TOKEN } # only needed for wildcards Firewall (ext/firewall; on whenever the config has firewall or rate_limits ). Peers outside allow_cidrs get 403. The client IP comes from client_ip_headers only when the peer is a trusted proxy, otherwise it is the peer. Rate-limited requests get 429 with Retry-After and a message naming the limit; every routed response carries -{Ip,Instance}-{Hourly,Concurrent}-{Limit,Remaining} and -{Ip,Instance}-Hourly-Reset , listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers . Long-lived responses (realtime) hold their concurrency slot until they end. TLS. Certificate files are core ( server.tls ). Automatic certificates are ext/autotls (its autotls section): with auto: true and no dns , every hostname the instance source maps gets its own certificate on its first TLS handshake (HTTP-01 / TLS-ALPN-01), with any DNS host and no API token; hostnames no instance serves never trigger issuance. A DNS provider (Cloudflare for now) is only needed for wildcard domains , proved through DNS-01; a wildcard without one is a config error. Each instance can override any of those limits (zero or missing fields keep the default): instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] limits: max_js_execution: 60s max_js_allocation: 128MiB id: api hosts: [api.example.com] access: { cors_origins: [https://app.example.com] } limits: { max_concurrent_js: 32 } extensions: firewall: { rate_limits: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_concurrent: 500 }, trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] }

title: Pocker
heading: Extensions
text: pocker.Provider.Extensions (or pocker.Server.Extensions in Go) takes extensions (see extension.go ). Each implements Name() and any of: extkit.Extension a PocketOne extension, registered on every instance's app before it bootstraps ( Register(app, cfg) ) with the instance's extensions. settings, its id in extkit.AppID(app) ; e.g. pitr, storage, tokens, s3redirect, mailrelay, bulkmail. enabled: false skips it for that instance. A change to an instance's extensions: settings restarts its app on its next request. The same value works on a single app. multisite.Extension a host extension ( RegisterHost ): it provides host contracts (gate/v1, tls/v1, http.wrap/v1, ...) as on any runtime (docs/extensions.md) Starter background work that needs pocker's Manager AppIniter host code that needs the whole Instance when setting up its app ( InitApp(inst, app) ); runs on every start, including restarts. Extensions use extkit.Extension instead, so they run on a single app too and pass the conformance test. Per-instance settings for an extension go under the instance's extensions. (read them with pocker.DecodeExtensionConfig ). app.Restart() (a backup restore, pitr) restarts only that instance, not the process. Timings for the Server-Timing header are registered with multisite.Timing(ctx, fn) . The stock pocketone binary runs pocker with mailtrap, and its host with servertiming and autotls ( multisite.Options.Extensions , the same under docker); the firewall turns on from its sections.

title: Pocker
heading: Platform values and logs
text: Superusers ( superusers: [{email, password_hash, id?, token_key?}] ) are upserted into the app's _superusers in Go when it starts, e.g. so a hosting platform's login works in the dashboard. Nothing goes through env. Private values ( private: {...} ) are for the host application's Go code and never visible to JS. A host registers that code with Server.SetupApp(inst, app) , which runs after migrations and before the app serves (for example a backup route checked against inst.Private["backup_token"] ). Secrets ( secrets: {...} ) are the instance's environment: what its JS sees through $os.getenv / process.env , and nothing else. No names are reserved; platform settings are explicit fields. Encryption key ( encryption_key ) encrypts the app's stored settings (like --encryptionEnv ). JS never sees it. Access ( access: {cors_origins} ) is the owner's say over which browser origins may call the instance (PocketBase matching: exact, , wildcards; empty = any). Client IPs that get the trusted rate limits are the firewall's extensions.firewall.trusted_ips (on top of the process-wide firewall.trusted_clients ). Extensions ( extensions: { : ...} ) are per-instance settings for extensions; extensions read them once, so changing them restarts the app on its next request. Logs: the app's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance in its pb_data . console. from JS hooks goes to /logs/exec.log as JSON lines {message, stream, time} ( stdout for log/info/debug, stderr for warn/error), rotated to exec.log.1 at 10 MiB. A start failure (e.g. a broken hooks file) is written there too, and only that instance fails. When an instance's secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , dev , dir , superusers , private or remote changes, a running app restarts (it stops, then a fresh one starts, as in a process restart), so a rotated secret takes effect immediately and two apps never have the instance's folder open. Host changes apply without a restart. GET /.well-known/health on any host reports {status, instances, running} . Changing an instance's files from host code (deploys, restores): Manager.WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn) stops the app, holds new requests for that instance, runs fn(dir) , then lets them through to a fresh app. Manager.StartInstance(ctx, id) starts it right away and returns the start error (for example to tell a deploy that a hook is broken), Manager.Running(id) says whether it is started, and Manager.InstanceDir(id) gives its folder. Manager.Ready() says whether the instance list has loaded. Manager.LogInstance(id, stream, message) appends to the instance's logs/exec.log (e.g. a scheduled job's result). Host code that runs in its own goroutines gets the Manager from Server.OnStart , before any request is served. Several servers, one set of instances. An instance with remote: runs on another server: Pocker checks the peer and the instance's rate limits here, then forwards the request (a reverse proxy to the URL by default; Server.Forward replaces it, e.g. to hold requests while the other server restarts). Its app never starts here, and an app already running here stops when remote is set. plain_listen gives the other servers a plain-HTTP port on a private network, and Manager.Firewall() lets host routes in front of the Manager use the same peer check.

title: Pocker
heading: Sandbox
text: Every instance's JS hooks and migrations run in a sandbox (the sandbox extension), and its SQL runs behind SQLite's authorizer ( sandbox/sqlguard.go ). The sandbox extension also owns the egress policy ( sandbox/egress.go ); pocker turns it on for its instances. sandbox_test.go runs one attack per route from one instance against another instance and the host; all of these are refused: Files: $os. , $filepath.glob/walk , $filesystem.fileFromPath , $template.loadFiles , $apis.static , require() Confined to the instance folder with an os.Root : the kernel resolves every path beneath it, refusing .. and symlinks that leave it. Relative paths and absolute paths inside the folder ( __hooks + "/x" ) work as before. Host primitives: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args , $filesystem.local Disabled ( $os.args is empty). Environment: $os.getenv , process.env Only the instance's own secrets . Go internals: $app.restart/bootstrap/runAllMigrations/onServe/onTerminate/onBootstrap/cron/unsafeWithoutHooks , hook.bindFunc/bind/trigger/unbind , sql.DB/Conn/Tx/Stmt (e.g. dbx.DB.DB() ), database/sql/driver , os/exec , net , syscall , http.Server controls Hidden from JS (the sandbox's member filter: they read as undefined , including when promoted from an embedded app type). Top-level onRecord , routerAdd , cronAdd and the rest of $app work as usual. Raw SQL ( $app.db().newQuery ) Allowed. SQLite's authorizer refuses ATTACH (and VACUUM INTO ) outside the instance's pb_data , PRAGMA temp_store_directory/data_store_directory and load_extension ; the CLI-only readfile / writefile / fsdir don't exist in the library. Statements without a deadline get max_query_duration . CPU Every JS call is interrupted after max_js_execution , Go calls included; sleep() is capped at 10 s. At most max_concurrent_js calls are in flight per instance. Memory Each instance has one QuickJS VM (ext/jsvm) with a hard cap (64 MiB by default): its JS heap plus the Go objects its JS holds. Growth past it, gradual or at once, is an out-of-memory error for that instance only. The JS stack is capped by size, so deep recursion is an error, never a crash. $os.readFile , fileFromPath and readerToString / toBytes are capped at max_js_allocation . Outbound network: $http.send , $filesystem.fileFromURL , S3 storage and backups, OAuth2/JWK fetches, SMTP Public addresses only, checked on the address actually connected to (after DNS, so rebinding doesn't help): loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata, CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges, and IPv6 equivalents/IPv4-in-IPv6 are refused unless listed in egress_allow . Installed process-wide on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client ( pocker/egress.go ). Host code that must reach private addresses (e.g. a control plane over a private network) uses its own http.Client with its own transport. $http.send timeouts and response bodies are capped. Limits of the memory controls: Go objects JS holds are charged by estimate, and Go's garbage collector can let the process use up to about twice the charge; set GOMEMLIMIT for the process as the backstop. Not covered yet: per-instance concurrency limits, and OS-level defence in depth: run Pocker as a non-root user with an OS firewall that only lets that user reach public addresses (a second, independent egress layer), plus seccomp and Landlock.

title: Pocker
heading: Changes to PocketBase
text: These live in the repo root (PocketBase's own files), not in this extension. Kept small and marked // PocketOne: so upstream merges stay easy: core.BaseAppConfig.AppMigrations : a per-app migrations list (JS migrations from jsvm register there instead of the global core.AppMigrations ). core.BaseAppConfig.EncryptionKey : the settings encryption key passed in directly instead of read from the process environment. The JS engine isn't a core change: Pocker runs jsvm (QuickJS), an extension, and the sandbox plugs into it. PocketBase's own plugins/jsvm is exactly upstream's. Mail needs no core change: the sandbox sends an app's own SMTP through the egress policy on OnMailerSend ( sandbox.BindMail ).

title: Pocker
heading: Versions
text: PocketOne has its own version line, starting at v0.0.1 , independent of PocketBase's numbers. When PocketBase releases, we merge it and decide then how to bump ours. Each release says which PocketBase version it's based on. The module path stays ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase , so a build pins a PocketOne version through the replace line: replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase = github.com/pockethost/pocketone v0.0.1

title: Remotes
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Named remotes for the pocketone command: the apps a project deploys to, each signed in to once. Give an app a name like prod , log in, and commands such as pocketone deploy prod know where to go and who you are. pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com pocketone login prod pocketone deploy prod # Deploy Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Remotes
heading: Install
text: Remotes is built into pocketone and on : the remote , login , logout and link commands are always there, and every app provides remote/v1: whoami at GET /api/_c/remote/v1 (so other machines can sign in to it), status, restart and logs. There's nothing to install: it's in the standard set. In your own Go build, use the standard set, or register it through its contracts yourself: app := pocketbase.New() extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{remotes.New(remotes.Config{})}, nil, nil) // remote/v1; on pocketbase.PocketBase also the commands app.Start() The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/remotes . Add Tokens for API tokens and the OAuth server for browser login.

title: Remotes
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen. Remotes keeps two files and reads a few environment variables.

title: Remotes
heading: The project's remotes
text: .pocketbase/remotes.json in the project holds names and URLs only, so commit it: {"default": "prod", "remotes": {"prod": {"url": "https://myapp.example.com"}}} Commands find it by walking up from the current folder. It isn't a pb_ name, since pb_ folders are deployed.

title: Remotes
heading: Saved logins
text: Logins are saved per user, keyed by URL, in ~/.config/pocketone/credentials.json (mode 0600). Set P1_CONFIG_DIR to use another folder; with XDG_CONFIG_HOME set, it's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pocketone/ .

title: Remotes
heading: Environment variables
text: P1_TOKEN_ A token for one remote, for CI. The name is upper case, other characters as _ ( P1_TOKEN_PROD ). P1_TOKEN A token for any remote. P1_CONFIG_DIR Where saved logins are kept. A token in the environment wins over a saved login. Every PocketOne variable starts with P1_ , in every build (the pockethost binary reads P1_TOKEN too). The pocketone folder comes from the command's name, so a build shipped under another name keeps its logins apart ( ~/.config/pockethost ).

title: Remotes
heading: Manage remotes
text: pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default pocketone remote list # names, URLs and who you're logged in as; marks the default pocketone remote default prod pocketone remote rm staging # the saved login stays; see logout pocketone remote whoami prod # who you are there, your token's scopes, and what the app offers A URL without a scheme gets https:// . The first remote you add becomes the default. A command that names no remote uses the default, else the only remote, else the one called default . Any command also takes a URL in place of a name: pocketone deploy https://other.example.com .

title: Remotes
heading: Log in
text: pocketone login prod login tries, in order (the command itself never asks for a password): The browser , when the remote runs the OAuth server. Your browser opens, you sign in and approve, and the command finishes. Over SSH or without a display it shows a code to enter on another device instead; --device asks for that, and --no-browser prints the URL without opening it. A pasted token ( pbt_... , a PocketHost token, or a PocketBase auth token). At the prompt, paste it, or pass --token or --token-stdin . A browser login keeps a refresh token and renews itself when it's within a day of expiring. You'll see Logged in to https://myapp.example.com as admin@example.com (oauth).

title: Remotes
heading: Link in one step
text: pocketone link https://myapp.example.com pocketone link https://myapp.pockethost.io ph_pat_... link adds the remote (named default , or --name ), makes it the default if there's none yet, and logs in. It takes the same login flags.

title: Remotes
heading: Log out
text: pocketone logout prod Forgets the saved login. A browser login is also revoked on the remote (its refresh token); a pasted token stays valid until you revoke it in the dashboard. If the remote can't be reached, it tells you to revoke it in the dashboard.

title: Remotes
heading: Works with
text: Deploy deploy , dev and pull resolve their remote and login through Remotes and find deploy/v1 in whoami's contracts; restart and logs use remote/v1. OAuth (in Tokens) Provides oauth/v1, so whoami lists it; login then signs in through the browser (loopback redirect on 127.0.0.1 with PKCE) or a device code. Tokens Provides the API tokens login takes when pasted. Whoami reports a token's id and scopes.

title: Remotes
heading: remote/v1
text: Remote control of an app, at /api/_c/remote/v1 : whoami GET /api/_c/remote/v1 none needed (any token may ask who it is) status GET /api/_c/remote/v1/status remote:read restart POST /api/_c/remote/v1/restart remote logs GET /api/_c/remote/v1/logs?n=100 (server-sent events) remote:read Whoami says who the request's credential is and what the app offers, so clients can discover it: {"auth": {"collection": "_superusers", "id": "…", "email": "admin@example.com"}, "via": "token", "tokenId": "…", "scopes": ["deploy", "remote"], "contracts": ["deploy/v1", "oauth/v1", "remote/v1", "tokens/v1"], "extensions": ["tokens", "remotes", "deploy"], "app": {"name": "Acme", "url": "https://myapp.example.com"}} via is token for an API token, jwt for a PocketBase auth token, and empty with no credential ( auth is then null , and extensions is left out). contracts are the contract APIs the app offers, each at /api/_c/ / : everything a client can use (oauth/v1's metadata is at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server ). Restart answers at once and restarts just after (under Pocker, only that instance).

title: Remotes
heading: Building on Remotes
text: remote/v1 client. remotev1.NewClient(url, token, httpClient) (ext/contracts/remote/v1) calls whoami, status, restart and logs. Go client. The CLI client lives with the contract, in remoteclient (ext/contracts/remote/v1/remoteclient), so other extensions' commands use it without importing this one. remoteclient.Open(dir, name) resolves a remote and its credential (environment first, then the saved login, renewing a browser login when due) and returns a remoteclient.Client : base URL, bearer token, an HTTP client with short connect timeouts, and JSON , NewRequest , Do and Whoami . It also holds the linked project ( LoadProject ), saved logins ( LoadCredentials ) and the sign-ins ( LoginWithToken , OAuthLogin ). Deploy's commands build on it. Commands. remotes.Commands() returns the remote , login , logout and link commands, for a binary that isn't a pocketbase.PocketBase . The rest of remote is generated: every operation of every contract the binary links is a remote ... command (cli.commands/v1), such as remote status , remote restart , remote restore to --at -2h . Login. remotes.BrowserLogin is the sign-in login tries first ( remoteclient.OAuthLogin ; tests replace it).

title: Remotes
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is an app with remotes and API tokens. Run two copies and add one as a remote of the other; its comment has the commands. // Command example is a PocketOne app with remotes and API tokens: run two copies, add one as a remote of the other's // project and sign in. // // go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 # the "remote" // go run ./example remote add local http://127.0.0.1:8090 # in a project folder // go run ./example login local # browser sign-in: admin@example.com / password // go run ./example remote whoami // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/remotes" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" // registered through their contracts (the standard set does this for you): remotes provides remote/v1 (whoami at // /api/_c/remote/v1, status, restart, logs) and the remote/login/logout/link commands; tokens adds API tokens // and the OAuth server login signs in through if _, err := extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{tokens.New(tokens.Config{}), remotes.New(remotes.Config{})}, nil, nil); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Fallback
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A default bucket for instances that have no S3 of their own. You name your S3-compatible backends once, then mount each kind of file on one: record uploads, backup zips, PITR history, or any extension's own kind. Every instance gets its own folder in the bucket and can't reach anything outside it. The credentials never reach the instance. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Install
text: S3 Fallback isn't built into pocketone ; add it to a Go build. Under Pocker, add it to the server's extensions: srv := &pocker.Server{Config: cfg, Extensions: []pocker.Extension{s3fallback.New(s3fallback.Config{})}} On a single app, register it with the backends and mounts in Go: extkit.MustRegister(app, s3fallback.New(s3fallback.Config{Backends: backends, Mounts: mounts})) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3-fallback .

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Configure
text: Under Pocker the storage section of pocketone.yaml is read at start. Fields set in Go win. storage: backends: # named S3-compatible destinations r2-eu: { endpoint: https:// .eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, bucket: pocketbase-eu, region: auto, access_key: $R2_KEY, secret: $R2_SECRET } b2-cold: { endpoint: ..., bucket: ph-backups, region: ..., access_key: ..., secret: ... } mounts: # filesystem kind - backend storage: r2-eu # record uploads backups: b2-cold # backup zips litestream: r2-eu # PITR history (ext/pitr) # enabled: false # off for every instance Each backend also takes prefix (prepended to every key, so several deployments can share a bucket) and force_path_style (for MinIO and similar servers). With no mounts the extension does nothing and files stay on local disk, as in PocketBase. Each instance can turn it off in its own settings, from instances.yaml or a mothership. Only enabled is read per instance; backends and mounts are the operator's: instances: id: blog extensions: { storage: { enabled: false } } The old shape ( bucket: with uploads: / backups: ) still works, with a warning: it becomes a backend named default , mounted for uploads and backups.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to do day to day. To an instance nothing is configured: Settings show S3 off, and uploads, thumbs, $app.newFilesystem() and the Backups screen work as before. Files land in the bucket under instances/ / / . Downloads stream through the server, or redirect to the bucket with S3 Redirect. When an instance turns on its own S3 (Settings → Files storage, or Settings → Backups), PocketBase's normal code takes over with the instance's credentials. Files already in the default bucket stay there, as PocketBase's own S3 switch doesn't move files either. It applies to instances created with the extension on. Files already on an instance's local disk are not read or moved.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Each instance gets the root instances/ / ; the storage section is read when the server starts. PITR Mount litestream and every instance without its own bucket keeps its history there. An instance's own PITR bucket still wins. S3 Redirect Downloads become signed redirects to the bucket. Nothing to wire: the fenced filesystem signs with its prefix, so S3 Redirect treats it like any S3 mount.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Building on S3 Fallback
text: Your own kind. Any kind an extension asks for through PocketBase's OnFilesystemCreate is served when it's mounted. PITR's litestream works this way. Uploads and backups step aside when the app turned on its own S3; for other kinds, the extension asking checks its own app setting first. Go API. Bind(app, root) serves an app's filesystems from the mounts under root ( "" for a single app, instances/ / under Pocker). FS(root, kind) returns the same fenced filesystem outside a hook; close it when done. Config() returns the effective configuration.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go yet. storage_test.go and mounts_test.go show it on a single app and under Pocker, against MinIO.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: How it works
text: PocketBase asks OnFilesystemCreate before it creates a filesystem. For a mounted kind, the extension answers with the backend, fenced to / . An instance can't list, read, write or delete anything outside it. The fence is a driver that adds the prefix to every key and strips it from listings. Signed download URLs are made with the backend's own credentials.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Status
text: Works and is tested against MinIO; not yet deployed.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: License

title: S3 Redirect
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree File downloads as short-lived signed redirects to your bucket, after PocketBase's own access check. When an app keeps its files in S3 (Settings → Files storage), PocketBase normally downloads each file from the bucket and streams it to the browser. With S3 Redirect, /api/files/... answers 302 with a presigned GET URL instead, and the browser fetches the file straight from the bucket. The app's bandwidth, memory and connections stay free. With Cloudflare R2 the downloads cost no egress either. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Install
text: S3 Redirect is built into pocketone and on by default . It only acts when S3 file storage is on: turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage and downloads redirect. With files on local disk, nothing changes. To stream files through the app as before: pocketone serve --s3Redirect=false In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: import "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect" app := pocketbase.New() s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) app.Start() Then turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Configure
text: Set it in pocketone.yaml : s3redirect: enabled: true # false streams files through the app ttl: 5m # how long each signed URL is valid Or with flags, which win over the file: --s3Redirect true Redirect downloads when S3 file storage is on. --s3Redirect=false streams them. --s3RedirectTTL 5m How long each signed URL stays valid (at most 7 days). Keep the TTL short: anyone holding a URL can fetch the file until it expires, protected files included. The bucket itself is PocketBase's own S3 setting, in Settings → Files storage . There are no other settings screens. Bucket CORS. A redirect followed by fetch() or from your site needs a CORS rule on the bucket allowing GET from your origin. Plain , and links need nothing.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: s3redirect:
text: Signed S3 redirects for file downloads: enabled, URL lifetime. The --s3Redirect and --s3RedirectTTL flags win. enabled bool On unless false (it only acts when S3 file storage is on). Flag: --s3Redirect. ttl duration How long each signed URL stays valid. Default 5m, max 7 days. Flag: --s3RedirectTTL.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Use
text: Once S3 is on, there's nothing to click. File URLs stay the same; they answer with a redirect: Access checks don't change. PocketBase still finds the record, checks protected-file tokens and the view rule, and creates thumbnails on first request. The redirect happens only after all of that. The file token stays private. It never goes into the bucket URL, and the redirect sends Referrer-Policy: no-referrer . Same headers as PocketBase: inline or attachment ( ?download=1 ), the filename, and forced content types (SVG, CSS, JS) are signed into the URL as S3 response- overrides. Range requests work, because S3 serves them. Caching: the browser may reuse the redirect for 80% of the TTL ( Cache-Control: private , never shared caches); the file itself gets PocketBase's usual 30-day Cache-Control . Falls back to streaming when S3 is off, the extension is turned off, or signing fails. A failed signature logs a warning, s3redirect: signing failed, streaming instead . Only GET and HEAD requests are redirected. Inline vs attachment: PocketBase decides this from the stored content type; S3 Redirect goes by the file extension (it doesn't ask the bucket, so a redirect costs no extra round trip). They agree for every file PocketBase names.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Try it
text: cd example && go run . serve The example runs one app with its own in-process bucket, nothing to set up. It: starts an S3-compatible bucket on 127.0.0.1:9199 (gofakes3, objects kept in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt ), and points the app's Files storage at it; seeds a demo_files record with an image (thumbs 100x100 ) and a protected text file, uploaded through PocketBase; prints the URLs to open. Each answers 302 to the bucket. The bucket only serves presigned GETs whose signature, re-computed with the AWS SDK's own SigV4 signer , matches and hasn't expired, and logs each one ( demo bucket: presigned GET ..., signature valid ). Unsigned or edited URLs get 403 . So a working download proves the signatures are AWS-compatible, not just accepted by a lenient fake. S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 skips the demo bucket (use your own Files storage settings); S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR moves it. The example is its own Go module, so its demo dependencies (gofakes3, the AWS SDK signer) never reach the extension's go.mod .

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Works with
text: Pocker The same extension runs on every instance. The s3redirect section sets the defaults; each instance can override enabled and ttl (below). S3 Fallback Apps without their own S3 settings keep files in its bucket (under pocker, fenced to instances/ /storage/ ). Its driver signs, so those downloads redirect too.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: srv.Extensions = append(srv.Extensions, s3redirect.New(s3redirect.Config{})) s3redirect: # server defaults enabled: true # on unless false ttl: 5m instances: id: abc extensions: s3redirect: { enabled: false } # per instance: enabled, ttl It's an extkit extension, so the same value works on a single app and on every pocker instance; it doesn't link pocker.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Building on S3 Redirect
text: Supply your own bucket. S3 Redirect signs for whatever filesystem PocketBase serves the download from: the app's own S3 settings, or one an extension supplies through OnFilesystemCreate . Implement s3redirect.Signer ( SignedURL(key, ttl, now, overrides) ) on your filesystem driver and its downloads redirect. Nothing else needs wiring; a filesystem that can't sign (local disk) streams as usual. Your own download handlers run first. The extension binds OnFileDownloadRequest last (priority 1000, id s3redirect.HookID , __ext_s3redirect__ ), so your Go or JS handlers can still change the served file or answer themselves without calling e.Next() . Unbind the id to turn it off for one app.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Example
text: example/main.go starts its own in-process S3 bucket, points the app's file storage at it and seeds a record, so every download redirect works with nothing to set up. Run go run . serve in example/ and open the URLs it prints. // Command example runs one PocketOne app whose file downloads redirect to an S3 bucket, with nothing to set up: // it starts its own S3-compatible bucket in-process (gofakes3, stored in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt), points the app's // Files storage at it, and seeds a "demo_files" record with an image and a protected document. // // go run . serve // // Open the URLs it prints. Each answers 302 with a signed URL; the bucket logs every fetch and only serves it if the // signature is valid and unexpired, checked independently with the AWS SDK's SigV4 signer. // // Set S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 to skip the demo bucket and use whatever Files storage you configure in the dashboard. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) if os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO") != "0" { addr := os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR") if addr == "" { addr = "127.0.0.1:9199" } registerDemo(app, addr) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Redirect
heading: How it works
text: Go module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect , no dependencies beyond PocketOne. The redirect is an OnFileDownloadRequest handler; the hook already exists upstream, so there's no core change. Signing is SigV4 query-string auth in sigv4 , checked against AWS's documented example. It needs no change to PocketBase's S3 client. The TTL is clamped to between 1 second and 7 days.

title: Sandbox
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Confines one PocketOne app's JS hooks and migrations, so apps from people you don't know can share one process. File access stays inside the app's folder, host primitives are gone, every JS call has a time limit, raw SQL can't leave the app's own database files, and outbound connections reach public addresses only. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Sandbox
heading: Install
text: Sandbox isn't a switch in pocketone : Pocker applies it to every instance it runs. With a multisite section in pocketone.yaml (pocker as the runtime), every instance is sandboxed and there's nothing to install. A single app served by pocketone without a multisite section is not sandboxed. In your own Go build, give it to the JSVM engine as an extension: sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{Dir: dir, Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}} execution, sleep := sb.Limits() jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []any{sb}, VM: jsvm.VMConfig{TaskWall: execution, MaxSleep: sleep}, }) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/sandbox . The SQL guard and the outbound network rules are separate calls (see Integrations).

title: Sandbox
heading: Configure
text: Sandbox has no pocketone.yaml section of its own. Under Pocker its limits are set in the pocker section, as defaults for every instance, and each instance can override them in its own limits : pocker: max_js_execution: 30s # each JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after this max_js_allocation: 64MiB # biggest single file read or reader JS can ask for max_call_stack_size: 2000 # unused: the JS engine caps its stack by size max_sleep: 10s # cap on sleep() max_query_duration: 30s # deadline for SQL statements that have none http_send_max_timeout: 60s # cap on $http.send timeouts http_send_max_body: 10MiB # cap on $http.send response size max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls one instance runs at once egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach, such as an internal SMTP relay The values shown are Pocker's defaults. An instance gets only its own secrets as environment. In a Go build, the same settings are Sandbox fields: Dir (required), Env , MaxExecution (default 30 s, negative turns it off), MaxSleep , MaxAllocation , HTTPSendMaxTimeout , HTTPSendMaxBody , and Console to send console. output somewhere other than the process's stdout and stderr. Limits() gives the execution and sleep limits for jsvm.Config.VM ; the memory cap and MaxConcurrent are set there too.

title: Sandbox
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to operate day to day. Hooks that stick to normal app code ( routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest) run unchanged. What changes for a hook author: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit and $filesystem.local fail with "not available on this host (sandboxed)"; $os.args is empty; process-wide Go methods such as $app.restart read as undefined . Files outside the app's folder can't be read or written, by any API, including through .. or symlinks. $os.getenv and process.env see only the app's own environment. A JS call that runs past its time limit is interrupted with an error; so is one that asks for a huge allocation. $http.send to a private or loopback address is refused. Under Pocker, console. output and hook errors go to the instance's own logs/exec.log .

title: Sandbox
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Runs every instance through the sandbox, the SQL guard and the outbound network rules, with limits from the pocker section and each instance's limits . Its attack tests are in sandbox_test.go . Multisite Carries the per-instance limits from instances.yaml or a mothership. Firewall Rate and concurrency limits in front of every request. Docker The alternative for untrusted apps: a container per instance instead of checks inside one process. Docker doesn't use the sandbox.

title: Sandbox
heading: Building on Sandbox
text: Sandbox is a jsvm extension ( OnInit , Modules , HTTPClient , and HideField / HideMethod to hide process-reaching Go members); add it to jsvm.Config.Extensions . GuardedDBConnect(maxQuery) is a core.DBConnectFunc : set it as the app's DBConnect to open the databases through SQLite's authorizer, with a deadline for statements that have none. InstallEgressPolicy(sandbox.EgressPolicy{Allow: ...}) routes Go's default HTTP transport through the public-only dialer, for the whole process. EgressPolicy.Dialer() gives the same check for your own connections. BindMail(app) sends the app's own SMTP through that dialer. ErrSandboxed is the error disabled bindings return.

title: Sandbox
heading: Example
text: One app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access confined to the app folder, host primitives disabled, and a 5 s limit per JS call. Run it from this folder with go run ./example serve . // Command example runs one PocketOne app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access is confined to the app folder, // host primitives ($os.exec, $os.exit, ...) are disabled, and every JS call has a time limit. // // go run ./example serve // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "path/filepath" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/sandbox" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" dir, _ := os.Getwd() sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{ Dir: dir, // JS may only touch this folder Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}, // the only environment JS sees MaxExecution: 5 time.Second, } jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []any{sb}, // OnInit, Modules, HTTPClient and the member filter }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Sandbox
heading: How is this safe?
text: With pocker, PocketOne can serve hundreds of instances from one Go process, each with its own owner, hooks and data. This section explains why that's safe enough to run code from people you don't know, and where it isn't. Configuration and the engine API are in POCKER.md. The attack tests are in sandbox_test.go .

title: Sandbox
heading: Why one process
text: Most hosted PocketBase instances are idle most of the time. A container per instance means paying idle memory and a cold start of a second or more for each one. In one process an instance's app starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, costs a few MB while it runs, and shares the Go runtime with everyone else. What you give up is the kernel boundary between tenants. Everything below replaces it with checks inside the process.

title: Sandbox
heading: The threat
text: Assume every instance's owner is hostile. They control: their pb_hooks (JavaScript, run by the instance's own QuickJS VM, ext/jsvm); their pb_migrations ; their collections, rules and settings; any SQL their hooks run; requests to their own instance. They must not be able to: read or change another instance's files, database, environment or settings; read the host's files, environment, credentials or private network; take the process down, or starve everyone else of CPU and memory.

title: Sandbox
heading: 1. Each instance is its own app
text: Every instance has its own core.App , database, settings, JS VMs, migrations list, settings encryption key and log. Requests are routed by hostname to exactly one app. Nothing in one app holds a reference to another. In production only hostnames the instance source maps are served; unknown hosts get 404 and never create a folder.

title: Sandbox
heading: 2. Files: confined by the kernel, not by string checks
text: Every file API reachable from JS goes through an os.Root opened on the instance's folder. That covers: $os. $filepath.glob / walk $filesystem.fileFromPath $template.loadFiles $apis.static require() The kernel resolves each path beneath that root and refuses .. and symlinks that lead out. There is no path string for an attacker to get clever with.

title: Sandbox
heading: 3. Host primitives: removed
text: The following are gone from JS: process control: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args ; $filesystem.local ; PocketBase internals that reach the whole process: $app.restart , bootstrap , onServe , onTerminate , raw hook triggers, sql.DB handles; Go's os/exec , net , syscall and database/sql/driver . A field-name mapper hides them, so they read as undefined . Everything a normal app uses still works: routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest.

title: Sandbox
heading: 4. Environment: only the instance's own
text: $os.getenv and process.env return the instance's own secrets and nothing else. Platform values never go through the environment: the settings encryption key; superusers the host keeps in sync; private tokens for the host's Go code.

title: Sandbox
heading: 5. SQL: SQLite's own authorizer
text: Raw SQL is allowed ( $app.db().newQuery(...) ), because PocketBase apps depend on it. Instead of parsing statements, PocketOne installs SQLite's authorizer callback on every connection, so SQLite itself refuses: ATTACH and VACUUM INTO outside the instance's pb_data ; load_extension ; the pragmas that move SQLite's files elsewhere. Statements without a deadline get one ( max_query_duration ).

title: Sandbox
heading: 6. Outbound network: public addresses only
text: PocketOne installs one dialer process-wide, on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client. It covers: $http.send $filesystem.fileFromURL S3 storage and backups OAuth2/JWKS fetches SMTP The dialer refuses: loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata; CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges; the IPv6 forms of all of these, including IPv4-in-IPv6. It checks the address actually connected to, after DNS, so DNS rebinding doesn't help. $http.send timeouts and response sizes are capped.

title: Sandbox
heading: 7. CPU, memory and concurrency
text: CPU Every JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after max_js_execution , Go calls included. sleep() is capped. Concurrency At most max_concurrent_js JS calls per instance in flight at once; more wait, then fail. Per-IP and per-instance rate and concurrency limits sit in front of every request. Memory Each instance's VM has a hard cap (default 64 MiB): the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds. A script that grows past it, slowly or at once, gets an out-of-memory error; other instances are unaffected. The JS stack is capped by size, so deep recursion is an error, never a crash. File reads are capped at max_js_allocation . Every limit has a process default and a per-instance override.

title: Sandbox
heading: 8. Failures stay with their instance
text: A broken hooks file, a panic during start or a failed migration fails that instance alone: it answers 502 and logs to its own logs/exec.log . Every other instance keeps serving. console. output goes to the instance's own log, never to the host's.

title: Sandbox
heading: What it doesn't cover
text: Be clear about these before you host strangers: Go memory is estimated. Go objects JS holds are charged to the instance by estimate, and Go's garbage collector can let the process use up to about twice that; set GOMEMLIMIT for the process. It's one address space. A bug in Go, QuickJS, SQLite or PocketOne's own checks would cross tenants in a way a container boundary wouldn't. The sandbox tests cover the known paths, but they don't prove nothing else exists. No OS-level layer yet. Seccomp, Landlock and a second, OS-level egress filter aren't built in.

title: Sandbox
heading: How to run it
text: For untrusted tenants, add the OS layers yourself: run PocketOne as a non-root user that owns only the instances folder; run it under a cgroup memory limit (with swap), so the worst case is a restart, not a host OOM; add an OS firewall rule that lets that user reach public addresses only, an egress layer independent of the process; keep secrets for host code out of the process environment; use private: values instead; put a proxy or the built-in firewall in front, with rate limits on. If you only run your own apps, the defaults are already more than stock PocketBase gives you.

title: Sandbox
heading: License
text: MIT

title: Schedules
text: Version 0.0.0 · Owners: @benallfree Scheduled webhooks per instance, called in-process even while the instance sleeps, with a catch-up run after downtime. Runs on: pocker (multitenant). Planned. Nothing is published here yet. title: Server Timing
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A Server-Timing response header on every request to an instance of a multisite host: how long the instance's own handler took, and how long it took to wake the instance for the request (under Pocker). Your browser's dev tools show it in the request's Timing tab. Server-Timing: origin;dur=12.4, wake;dur=0.0 Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Server Timing
heading: Install
text: Server Timing is built into pocketone and on whenever it serves many instances, whatever the provider. There's nothing to install. It isn't used for a single app. In your own host build, list it first among the host extensions, so its header covers every other hop: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Extensions: []multisite.Extension{servertiming.New() / , other host extensions /}}) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/servertiming .

title: Server Timing
heading: Configure
text: There's nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen.

title: Server Timing
heading: Use
text: Open your browser's dev tools, pick a request to an instance and look at its timing, or read the header with curl: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/health grep -i server-timing origin The instance's own handler: from handing it the request until it sent its response headers. wake Starting the instance for this request. 0 when it was already running. Each value is in milliseconds, one decimal, up to the response headers (time to first byte). The innermost hop comes first; values a server in front already sent are kept, and this host's entries are added after them.

title: Server Timing
heading: Integrations
text: Pocker registers origin and wake for every request it hands to an instance. Add your own entries. Host code and other extensions call multisite.Timing(ctx, fn) during a request; fn returns []multisite.TimingEntry{{Name, Dur, Desc}} and runs when the headers go out. Only extensions listed after Server Timing are covered. Put names in Desc , never addresses. Go API. FormatTiming , AppendServerTiming and WithServerTiming render entries, append them to a header and wrap a response writer, for a server that isn't a multisite host.

title: Server Timing
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go . See it used in examples/pocketone/multi.go , which lists it first in the pocketone binary's host extensions.

title: Server Timing
heading: How it works
text: It's a host wrapper ( multisite.Wrapper ). For each request it starts collecting timing entries in the request's context, then stamps them into the Server-Timing header just before the response headers go out (not on interim 1xx responses). Flush, Hijack and http.ResponseController keep working through its writer.

title: Standard Set
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree The extensions every PocketOne app has: settings, page templates, a cache, API tokens (with the OAuth server), remotes (remote/v1), MCP, PocketPages, S3 redirects, point-in-time restore, backups, bulk mail and deploy. The stock pocketone binary and every Pocker instance use it, so an app never misses one because its host forgot to list it. Members can be reconfigured or turned off per app, never removed. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Standard Set
heading: Install
text: The standard set is built into pocketone . In your own Go build, make the app with it instead of pocketbase.New() : set := standard.New() app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"}) app.Start() NewApp registers the members, loads pb_hooks with their JS APIs ( $mcp , $tokens , $bulkmail ) and resolves their contracts. On an app you built yourself, call set.Register(app, jsvmConfig) instead.

title: Standard Set
heading: Configure
text: Reconfigure a member: replace it, e.g. set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 24 time.Hour}) . A member set to nil is an error. Turn one off: enabled: false in its pocketone.yaml section, or in an instance's extensions. under Pocker. Extensions that require it turn off too, and say why. Add your own: set.Add(myextension.New()) . Extras register after the members, under the same rules. Pick providers: set.Providers is pocketone.yaml 's providers: section, for a contract more than one extension provides.

title: Standard Set
heading: providers:
text: Which extension provides a contract when several do.

title: Standard Set
heading: Use
text: Each app logs what it got when it starts: standard: on: settings, templates, cache, tokens, remotes, mcp, pages, s3redirect, pitr, backups, bulkmail, deploy standard: tokens/v1 ← tokens With remotes off (deploy requires its remote/v1): standard: remotes off: enabled: false standard: deploy off: needs remote/v1, which nothing provides

title: Standard Set
heading: Integrations
text: Pocker Every instance gets the set ( Server.Standard ), with its own extensions. settings. Contracts Members find each other through contracts ( tokens/v1 ), resolved per app; the startup lines show who provides what.

title: Standard Set
heading: Example
text: // A PocketOne app with the standard set and one extra extension: run it with go run . serve . package main import ( "log" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pitr" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/standard" ) func main() { set := standard.New() set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 24 time.Hour}) // reconfigure a member set.Add(mailtrap.New()) // add your own app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }
